laws.title: Drink Driving — 0.8g/L BAC (Mexico City)
laws.subtitle: Varies by state — CDMX strictly enforced
laws.fullDescription: Mexico City enforces 0.8g/L BAC limit. Many states have 0.4g/L or zero tolerance. Operativos (roadside checks) common at night and holidays.
laws.penalty: Above limit: fine of 30 days minimum wage + licence suspension + possible criminal charges + vehicle impound.
exceptions: Some states have no formal equipment for testing yet

quiz.q: Blood alcohol limit for drivers in Mexico City (CDMX)?
quiz.explanation: Mexico City enforces a 0.8g/L (0.08% BAC) drink-drive limit.

laws.title: Mexican Greetings — Warmth and Abrazo
laws.subtitle: Abrazo, cheek kiss, Don/Doña for elders
laws.fullDescription: Mexicans are warm and expressive. Friends and family: abrazo (hug) + right cheek kiss. Business: firm handshake initially, warms up quickly. 'Don' / 'Doña' before first names shows respect for elders. Being late up to 15–30 minutes is culturally accepted for social events (though not for business meetings).
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — being cold or overly punctual to social events can seem rigid.
exceptions: Northern Mexico is more formal and punctual
Government/corporate meetings expect punctuality

quiz.q: What do 'Don' and 'Doña' indicate before a first name in Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Don/Doña before a first name (e.g. Don Carlos) is a respectful address for elders in Mexico.

laws.title: Mordida — Bribery of Officials is Illegal
laws.subtitle: Anti-Corruption Laws — Paying bribes increases legal risk
laws.fullDescription: 'Mordida' (the bite) refers to bribes commonly expected by some corrupt officials. While it may seem expected, paying a bribe to a police officer or official is illegal in Mexico and can be used as evidence against you. Tourist advisory: if stopped by police and asked for money, ask for a formal ticket (infracción). Never hand over your passport — ask to go to the station instead.
laws.penalty: Paying a bribe: potential corruption charges. Extortion by officials: report to CEAPP. Giving in increases vulnerability to repeat targeting.
exceptions: Official fines paid to the government treasury are legal
Always ask for an official receipt (recibo) for any payment
laws.sourceLabel: Ley General del Sistema Nacional Anticorrupción

quiz.q: What should you do if a Mexican police officer asks for money (mordida)?
options: Ask for a formal traffic ticket (infracción) instead
quiz.explanation: Paying mordida is illegal and marks you as an easy target. Request a formal infracción (ticket) paid to the government — this is your legal right.

laws.title: Tequila & Mezcal — Protected Designations of Origin
laws.subtitle: NOM-006 — Fake tequila is a serious issue; check the label
laws.fullDescription: Tequila and mezcal are protected designations of origin in Mexico. Real tequila must be made from blue agave in designated regions (primarily Jalisco) and bear a CRT (Consejo Regulador del Tequila) seal with a NOM number. Counterfeit tequila (sometimes containing methanol) is a real health risk at some tourist venues. Always check for the official label.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty for tourists buying fake tequila — but serious health risk. Producers of fake tequila face criminal charges.
exceptions: Licensed distilleries with CRT certification
Official duty-free purchases

quiz.q: What should you check on a tequila bottle to verify it is genuine?
quiz.explanation: Genuine Mexican tequila carries a CRT (Consejo Regulador del Tequila) seal and a NOM registration number — counterfeits may lack these and can contain dangerous methanol.

laws.title: Cartel Safety Warning — High-Risk Zones and Travel Advisories
laws.subtitle: SESNSP data — Some regions no-go for tourists; kidnapping risk
laws.fullDescription: While Mexico is safe for tourists in major resorts and cities, significant parts of the country are under travel advisories due to cartel activity. The US State Department rates several Mexican states as 'Do Not Travel' (Level 4) — including Colima, Guerrero, Michoacán, Tamaulipas, and Zacatecas. Even in relatively safe zones, driving at night on rural roads is dangerous. Express kidnapping (where victims are forced to withdraw ATM funds) occurs. Always register with your country's embassy and use official transport.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty for tourists — but ignoring safety advisories exposes visitors to genuine kidnapping and cartel violence risk.
exceptions: Major resort areas (Cancún, Los Cabos, Puerto Vallarta) generally safe with normal precautions
Organised tour groups with security protocols
laws.sourceLabel: US State Department — Mexico Travel Advisory

quiz.q: What level travel warning does the US State Department issue for states like Guerrero and Tamaulipas in Mexico?
quiz.explanation: States like Guerrero (Acapulco), Tamaulipas, and Colima carry a US Level 4 'Do Not Travel' advisory due to cartel violence — while major tourist resorts carry lower advisory levels.

laws.title: Mexico City Property and Housing Rights — Colonias and Ejido Land
laws.subtitle: Ley Agraria — Ejido communal land has complex legal status
laws.fullDescription: Mexico has a complex dual land ownership system. Ejido land (communally held agrarian land originating from post-revolution land reform) cannot be sold like private property without a formal conversion process. In Mexico City and other urban areas, many informal settlements ('colonias populares') sit on ejido land — which can mean complex title issues. Foreigners cannot directly own land within 50km of the coast or 100km of a border (the 'Restricted Zone') without setting up a fideicomiso (bank trust) or a Mexican corporation. This catches many foreign property buyers off guard.
laws.penalty: Building on ejido land without proper conversion: risk of demolition order. Foreign direct ownership in Restricted Zone: void/illegal transaction.
exceptions: Fideicomiso (bank trust) allows foreigners to effectively control Restricted Zone property
Mexican corporations owned by foreigners can hold restricted zone property
laws.sourceLabel: Ley Agraria — Secretaría de Agricultura Mexico

quiz.q: How can foreigners legally own property in Mexico's coastal Restricted Zone (50km from coast)?
options: Direct ownership is allowed for all foreigners
Through a fideicomiso (bank trust) or Mexican corporation
Foreigners cannot own any coastal property at all
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Restricted Zone prohibits foreigners from directly owning coastal or border land — but a fideicomiso (bank trust arrangement) allows foreigners to effectively control and benefit from such property.

laws.title: Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) — Sacred Cultural Heritage; Respectful Participation Only
laws.subtitle: UNESCO Intangible Heritage — Altars (ofrendas) are sacred; not a Halloween party
laws.fullDescription: Day of the Dead (Días de Muertos, November 1–2) is a UNESCO-recognised Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The holiday honours deceased family members with altars (ofrendas) decorated with marigolds (cempasúchil), photos, food offerings, and candles. Mexico City's large cemetery processions and Oaxaca's radish festival are globally famous. However, the commercialisation and 'Halloween-isation' of the holiday has become a sensitive issue — particularly for indigenous communities in Oaxaca, Michoacán, and southern Mexico. Visitors who participate should do so respectfully: do not treat grave visits as photo opportunities without permission from families, do not wear costume sugar skull makeup as a joke, and ask before joining private family vigils.
laws.penalty: No criminal law against disrespectful tourism, but social sanction is strong. Vandalism of cemetery altars: criminal damage to property.
exceptions: Organised cultural tourism tours with community approval
Invited participation by a Mexican family is the ideal way to experience the holiday authentically
laws.sourceLabel: UNESCO — Day of the Dead: Intangible Cultural Heritage

quiz.q: On which dates is Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) traditionally celebrated in Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Día de Muertos is celebrated on November 1 (Día de Todos Santos — All Saints' Day, for children) and November 2 (Día de los Muertos — for adults) — distinct from Halloween on October 31.

laws.title: Whale Shark and Whale Watching — Strict Approach Distances; Isla Contoy Rules
laws.subtitle: NOM-131-SEMARNAT-2010 — Whale sharks: 3m minimum distance; no touching
laws.fullDescription: Mexico hosts some of the world's largest whale shark aggregations — particularly off Isla Holbox and Isla Mujeres in the Yucatán Peninsula. Mexico's NOM-131-SEMARNAT-2010 strictly regulates cetacean and whale shark tourism: a minimum 3-metre approach distance, no touching, no flash photography, snorkellers may enter the water but only with certified guides, and only 2 snorkellers per whale shark are allowed at one time. Whale watching tours must be licensed by SEMARNAT and CONANP. Grey whale watching in Baja California's San Ignacio and Ojo de Liebre lagoons (UNESCO World Heritage) requires official permits — the lagoons are critical calving areas. Violating marine mammal protection rules is a federal offence.
laws.penalty: Touching a whale shark or whale: fine up to MXN $870,000. Unlicensed whale watching tour: licence revocation + criminal charge.
exceptions: Licensed marine biologists with SEMARNAT research permits
Emergency situations involving injured animals

quiz.q: Under Mexico's NOM-131-SEMARNAT-2010, what is the minimum approach distance for snorkellers near whale sharks?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's whale shark regulations require a minimum 3-metre approach distance for snorkellers — with only 2 people allowed in the water per whale shark at a time and no touching under any circumstances.

laws.title: Sea of Cortez Protected Biosphere — Fishing, Tourism, and Vaquita Porpoise Emergency Rules
laws.subtitle: Mexico's 'Aquarium of the World' has emergency closures; vaquita porpoise critically endangered
laws.fullDescription: The Gulf of California (Sea of Cortez) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site described by Jacques Cousteau as 'the world's aquarium.' Mexico's biosphere reserve regulations prohibit unauthorized fishing, jet ski use, and anchoring on coral in protected zones. The vaquita porpoise — the world's most critically endangered marine mammal with fewer than 10 individuals remaining — is driving emergency measures. PROFEPA (Federal Environmental Protection Agency) conducts active patrols. Gillnet fishing (which entangles vaquitas) is banned across the entire Upper Gulf of California. Despite bans, illegal totoaba fish bladder poaching (for Chinese traditional medicine black markets worth $20,000+ per bladder) continues. Navy and Sea Shepherd vessels actively intercept illegal fishing boats.
laws.penalty: Illegal fishing in protected zones: fines up to MXN 50,000 (~$3,000) + vessel confiscation. Totoaba trafficking: up to 9 years imprisonment + MXN 300,000 fines. Unauthorized anchoring on coral: MXN 5,000–20,000.
exceptions: Traditional coastal communities with established fishing rights in buffer zones
Scientific research vessels with CONANP permits
Eco-tourism operators with SEMARNAT certification
laws.sourceLabel: CONANP — Gulf of California Biosphere Reserve

quiz.q: Approximately how many vaquita porpoises — the world's most critically endangered marine mammal — are believed to remain?
quiz.explanation: As of 2023, fewer than 10 vaquita porpoises are believed to survive, making it the world's most critically endangered marine mammal. Despite Mexican navy patrols and Sea Shepherd conservation efforts, illegal gillnet fishing continues to threaten the species with imminent extinction.

laws.title: GMO Corn Ban — Mexico Restricted Genetically Modified Corn to Protect Native Varieties
laws.subtitle: Mexico issued 2020 decree phasing out GM corn imports; US trade dispute followed
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 2020 presidential decree (Decreto DOF 31/12/2020) ordered a gradual phase-out of GM corn imports and the herbicide glyphosate, aiming for complete elimination by January 2024. The decree cited protection of the 59+ native Mexican corn (maíz criollo) varieties, Mayan and Indigenous food sovereignty, and precautionary health concerns. Mexico is the origin center of corn's domestication (approximately 9,000 years ago) — hundreds of native varieties represent irreplaceable genetic heritage. The US challenged the decree under USMCA trade rules, arguing it violated free trade commitments. An arbitration panel partly ruled against Mexico in 2023, requiring scientific justification. Mexico partially modified the decree but maintained restrictions on GM corn for human tortilla consumption while allowing GM corn for animal feed with conditions.
laws.penalty: Importing non-authorized GM corn (under decree as applied): administrative confiscation + fines. Planting unauthorized GM crops without SENASICA permit: fines up to MXN 400,000 (~$24,000).
exceptions: GM corn for animal feed imports with SENASICA authorization (partially maintained)
Certified research institutions studying GM corn varieties
Traditional seed banks documenting native varieties
laws.sourceLabel: Mexico DOF — GM Corn Decree December 2020

quiz.q: Why is Mexico particularly concerned about protecting its native corn varieties?
options: Mexican corn is the most nutritious in the world by scientific measurement
Mexico is the origin center of corn's domestication 9,000 years ago with 59+ irreplaceable native varieties
Mexican corn has unique flavors protected by geographical indication
Foreign corn varieties cause crop diseases that threaten food security
quiz.explanation: Mexico is the origin center of corn domestication — corn (maíz) was first cultivated from wild teosinte in Mexico approximately 9,000 years ago. Mexico has 59+ native corn varieties representing irreplaceable genetic heritage, making it uniquely important to protect against genetic dilution or contamination from commercial GM varieties.

laws.title: Mexico's 2024 Judicial Reform — Elected Judges and Supreme Court Overhaul
laws.subtitle: Mexico voted to elect all federal judges by popular vote in 2024; a world first with major rule of law concerns
laws.fullDescription: President Claudia Sheinbaum's 2024 constitutional reform — carried over from Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO) — amended Mexico's constitution to require that all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, be elected by popular vote. Mexico became the first country in the world to elect its entire federal judiciary by direct vote. Critics (including the US Embassy, legal scholars, the Mexican Bar Association, and judicial employees who protested extensively) argued elected judges would be more susceptible to political pressure, cartel influence, and populist pressure. Supporters argued it would democratize a corrupt, elite-controlled judiciary. Existing federal judges were automatically terminated; new elections were set for June 2025. The US and Canada raised concerns under USMCA about rule of law implications.
laws.penalty: Judges campaigning in violation of new election rules: electoral authority sanctions. Attempting to influence judicial elections: electoral crimes.
exceptions: State-level judges follow different processes in many states
Military courts are not included in the popular election reform
Transition provisions for sitting judges during the implementation phase
laws.sourceLabel: Mexico Official Gazette — Judicial Reform Constitutional Amendment 2024

quiz.q: What made Mexico's 2024 judicial reform a world first?
options: It created the world's largest supreme court
All federal judges including Supreme Court justices must be elected by popular vote
It established mandatory gender parity on all federal courts
It gave Indigenous communities power to elect their own federal judges
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 constitutional reform made it the first country in the world to require that all federal judges — including Supreme Court justices — be elected by direct popular vote. Critics argued this unprecedented system would expose judges to political and cartel influence, while supporters said it would democratize an elite, corrupt judiciary.

laws.title: Femicide Crisis & Gender Alert Mechanism
laws.subtitle: Mexico averages 10 women murdered per day; femicide is a specific criminal category with enhanced sentences
laws.fullDescription: Mexico codified femicide as a distinct crime in 2012 — the killing of a woman because of her gender — carrying 40–70 years imprisonment, higher than ordinary homicide. Despite this, approximately 10 women are murdered daily in Mexico; the official count was 940 femicides in 2022. The Gender Violence Alert mechanism allows civil society to petition for emergency government action in specific states. Forced disappearances of women are a parallel crisis: over 4,000 women are reported missing annually. The #UnDiaSinNosotras ('One Day Without Us') strike on March 9, 2020 saw millions of women absent from work and school, leaving cities visibly empty.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 40–70 years imprisonment. Attempted femicide: 16–30 years. Gender violence alerts allow states to face additional federal oversight and resource requirements.
exceptions: Indigenous customary law communities have separate jurisdiction for some cases under UNAM guidance
Witness protection programs exist for domestic violence victims who testify against abusers
Femicide classification requires demonstrating gender motive — prosecutors often prefer ordinary homicide charges
laws.sourceLabel: CONAVIM — National Commission to Prevent Violence Against Women

quiz.q: When was femicide codified as a distinct crime with enhanced penalties in Mexico's federal criminal law?
quiz.explanation: Mexico codified femicide — the killing of a woman because of her gender — as a distinct crime in 2012, carrying 40–70 years imprisonment. Despite this, approximately 10 women continue to be murdered daily in Mexico.

laws.title: Claudia Sheinbaum — Mexico's First Female President
laws.subtitle: A climate scientist became Mexico's first female president, inheriting AMLO's judicial overhaul
laws.fullDescription: On June 2, 2024, Claudia Sheinbaum won Mexico's presidential election with 59% — the largest margin in modern Mexican democracy — becoming Mexico's first female president and the first with a PhD (environmental engineering from Berkeley). She succeeded Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO), whose Morena party she leads. Before taking office October 1, 2024, AMLO passed a controversial constitutional reform eliminating Mexico's independent judiciary and replacing appointed judges with elected ones — the first such system in the world. Sheinbaum inherited both AMLO's popular mandate and his democratic erosion concerns. She faced immediate tension with the US over fentanyl, migration, and cartels.
laws.penalty: AMLO's judicial reform: judges who refuse to participate in elections face removal. US retaliation for cartels operating freely: potential sanctions. Mexico's anti-femicide laws carry enhanced sentences of 40–70 years for gender-motivated killings.
exceptions: The Supreme Court challenged parts of the judicial reform before new judges were elected
US-Mexico relations operate under the T-MEC/USMCA trade agreement framework
Sheinbaum pledged continuity on major infrastructure projects (Tren Maya, Felipe Ángeles airport)

quiz.q: What unprecedented electoral change did AMLO implement in Mexico's judiciary before leaving office?
options: He abolished the Supreme Court entirely
He created a judicial dictatorship with lifetime judges
He replaced appointed judges with elected judges — the first such system in the world
He merged the judiciary with the executive branch
quiz.explanation: AMLO's 2024 constitutional reform replaced Mexico's independent appointed judiciary with an elected judiciary — the first country in the world to elect judges at all levels, including Supreme Court justices, through popular vote — a change widely criticized as undermining judicial independence.

laws.title: Alerta de Género: Mexico's Femicide Emergency Alert System
laws.subtitle: Mexico activates state-level gender violence emergencies when femicide rates spike — but implementation remains deeply flawed
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's General Law on Women's Access to a Life Free of Violence (2007) created the Alerta de Violencia de Género (Gender Violence Alert) mechanism — a declaration that triggers emergency resources and special prosecutors when femicide rates in a state become crisis-level. Mexico records approximately 10 women killed daily, and femicide (murder with gender motive) is a specific crime in all 32 states carrying 40–70 years imprisonment. Despite the laws, only a fraction of femicide cases result in conviction. The 2020 feminist protests — including hammering nails and glitter bombs at the National Palace — pressured President AMLO's government for stronger enforcement.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 40–70 years imprisonment (varies by state). Gender violence alerts trigger mandatory emergency response protocols for state governments
exceptions: The federal and state definitions of femicide vary, creating jurisdictional confusion
Intimate partner killings classified as 'passion crimes' by some prosecutors still evade femicide charges
laws.sourceLabel: CONAVIM – Mexico National Commission to Prevent Violence Against Women

quiz.q: Approximately how many women are killed per day in Mexico, making it one of the world's worst countries for femicide?
quiz.explanation: Mexico records approximately 10 women killed daily, placing it among the world's highest femicide rates. Despite laws carrying 40–70 year sentences, conviction rates remain extremely low.

laws.title: Mexico's Judicial Reform: Elected Judges & Supreme Court Overhaul
laws.subtitle: President Sheinbaum's government overhauled Mexico's judiciary by making all judges subject to popular election — a move critics called a democratic rollback
laws.fullDescription: In September 2024, outgoing President AMLO passed a sweeping judicial reform — making Mexico the first major country to require all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote. The reform also reduced the Supreme Court from 11 to 9 members and created new oversight bodies. Thousands of judges and court workers struck in protest; the opposition walked out of Congress; and US officials expressed concern. Critics argued the reform would politicize the judiciary and weaken independence. Supporters argued Mexico's judicial system was corrupt and elitist. The first judicial elections were held in 2025. International investors cited the reform as a risk factor for Mexico's business climate.
laws.penalty: No direct criminal penalties for citizens — this is a constitutional restructuring. Judges who refused to comply with transition timelines faced forced retirement
exceptions: The Electoral Tribunal (TEPJF) operates under modified rules
Some specialized tribunals have different transition timelines
laws.sourceLabel: Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation – Mexico

quiz.q: What made Mexico's 2024 judicial reform unprecedented among major countries?
options: It eliminated the Supreme Court entirely
It required all federal judges — including Supreme Court justices — to be elected by popular vote
It gave the president power to directly appoint all judges
It created a system of international arbitration for all disputes
quiz.explanation: Mexico became the first major country in the world to require all federal judges — from local courts up to Supreme Court justices — to be elected by popular vote, rather than appointed through merit-based processes. Critics argued this fundamentally compromises judicial independence.

laws.title: Femicide Law
laws.subtitle: Mexico's penal code recognizes femicide as a distinct, aggravated homicide
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Federal Penal Code (Article 325) defines femicide (feminicidio) as the killing of a woman because of her gender — including killings involving violence, degradation, or involving intimate partner or family relationships. Femicide carries 40–70 years imprisonment, higher than ordinary homicide. Mexico averages over 10 women murdered per day, with many cases involving organized crime. Several states have declared 'gender violence alerts' (alertas de género) that trigger special protective measures. Despite the law, impunity rates for femicide remain extremely high — UNAM studies found that over 90% of cases go unsolved.
laws.penalty: 40 to 70 years imprisonment; no parole for the most serious cases; perpetrators lose parental rights
exceptions: The femicide definition requires proof of gender-based motive; without this, cases are prosecuted as ordinary homicide with lower sentences

quiz.q: What is the legal definition of femicide (feminicidio) under Mexican law?
options: Any murder committed with a weapon
The killing of a woman because of her gender
Murder of a female family member
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Penal Code defines femicide specifically as the killing of a woman because of her gender, often evidenced by signs of sexual violence, degradation, or prior abuse by an intimate partner or family member.

laws.title: GMO Corn Ban
laws.subtitle: Mexico banned genetically modified corn to protect indigenous varieties and tortilla culture
laws.fullDescription: Mexico issued a presidential decree in 2020 (modified 2023) phasing out genetically modified corn for human consumption and the herbicide glyphosate. Mexico is the center of origin of corn (maize) — over 59 native varieties exist there — and the government argued GMO corn threatens biodiversity, indigenous agricultural traditions, and the tortilla culture at the heart of Mexican food. The US and Canada challenged the ban under the USMCA trade agreement, arguing it violated free trade rules. A USMCA dispute panel ruled against parts of Mexico's ban in 2023, forcing some modifications, but Mexico maintained restrictions on direct human consumption of GMO corn.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized cultivation or sale of GMO corn for human consumption: fines under biosafety law; commercial violations: product recalls
exceptions: GMO corn for animal feed and industrial uses is allowed
Authorized scientific research is exempt

quiz.q: How many native varieties of corn (maize) exist in Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Mexico is the center of origin of corn (Zea mays) and has over 59 distinct native (criollo) varieties — a genetic diversity that the GMO corn ban aims to protect from cross-pollination by transgenic strains.

laws.title: Judicial Reform 2024
laws.subtitle: Mexico's Lopez Obrador rewrote the judiciary — all judges now elected by popular vote
laws.fullDescription: In September 2024, Mexico's congress passed President Lopez Obrador's controversial judicial reform, amending the constitution to require that all Supreme Court justices, federal judges, and magistrates be elected by popular vote rather than appointed. The reform eliminates the judiciary's ability to strike down congressional acts through a constitutional review process and was opposed by the US, the Mexican Bar Association, the UN, and thousands of Mexican judges who went on strike. Mexico's Supreme Court justices will be elected in June 2025 with candidates nominated by Congress, the executive, and judiciary. Critics argue it destroys judicial independence by subjecting judges to electoral politics.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional amendment; violations of the new electoral process for judges would be prosecuted under electoral law
exceptions: The reform has transitional provisions — existing Supreme Court justices must resign and run for election or leave

quiz.q: What makes Mexico's 2024 judicial reform unique in the world?
options: It created a separate constitutional court
It required all judges to be lawyers
It made all federal judges elected by popular vote
It gave the military authority over criminal courts
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 judicial reform requires all Supreme Court justices, federal judges, and magistrates to be elected by popular vote — an arrangement found nowhere else in the world at this scale. Critics argue it destroys judicial independence by making judges answer to electoral pressures.

laws.title: Judicial Reform: Election of Judges by Popular Vote (2024)
laws.subtitle: Mexico's constitutional reform to elect all federal judges directly was unprecedented globally
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted a sweeping judicial reform in September 2024 under President Claudia Sheinbaum (succeeding Andrés Manuel López Obrador's MORENA party). The reform, passed after controversial legislative maneuvering including moving sessions to avoid opposition disruption, amended the constitution to: require all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote (beginning in 2025 for part of the judiciary); reduce the Supreme Court from 11 to 9 justices; abolish the Federal Judiciary Council and replace it with a new oversight body; and introduce disciplinary mechanisms for judges. The reform was extraordinarily controversial: sitting judges protested in the streets, law students went on strike, the U.S. Embassy expressed concern, Canada recalled its ambassador for consultations, and the peso fell significantly. Critics argue electing judges undermines judicial independence; supporters argue it makes the judiciary accountable to the people.
laws.penalty: Judges who interfere with the electoral process for judicial elections: criminal prosecution; the new discipline tribunal has powers to remove and sanction judges
exceptions: State judiciary remains under separate state constitutional frameworks
Military courts have separate reform track
Electoral tribunal has special transitional provisions

laws.title: Femicide Law and Gender Violence Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: Mexico has among the world's highest rates of femicide despite having specific femicide criminal laws
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted femicide as a specific criminal offense in 2007 (General Law on Access of Women to a Life Free from Violence) and incorporated femicidio into the Federal Penal Code (Article 325) in 2012. A femicidio conviction requires proof that the killing was 'motivated by gender' — a higher legal bar than ordinary homicide. Despite this legal framework, Mexico has one of Latin America's highest femicide rates: approximately 10-11 women are killed per day in Mexico (official counts, which rights groups say significantly undercount). In 2020, the feminist movement ('marea verde,' building on the Ni Una Más movement) organized major marches and an unprecedented women's strike (9M) on March 9, 2020. The Emergency Alert for Gender Violence (Alerta de Violencia de Género, AVG) mechanism allows states to declare emergencies triggering federal support — but activists argue these have been ineffective. Mexico's National Guard and army involvement in security has complicated accountability.
laws.penalty: Femicidio: 40–70 years imprisonment (plus aggravating circumstances); gender-based torture: separate penalties; failure by officials to investigate with gender perspective: administrative sanctions
exceptions: Self-defense in domestic violence contexts has been applied to reduce sentences for women who killed abusers
Some states have specific femicidio protocols providing victim support
Minors who commit gender violence are handled through juvenile justice system

laws.title: 2024 Judicial Reform and Elected Judges
laws.subtitle: Mexico controversially passed a law requiring direct election of all judges
laws.fullDescription: In September 2024, outgoing President Andrés Manuel López Obrador pushed through a sweeping judicial reform making Mexico the first country in the world to elect all federal judges — including Supreme Court justices — by popular vote. The reform was passed amid protests from judges, lawyers, and civil society, including a strike by federal court employees. Critics argued it would subject judges to political and criminal influence, potentially enabling organized crime to elect favorable judges. The US and Canada expressed concern about rule-of-law implications for the USMCA trade agreement. Incoming President Claudia Sheinbaum defended the reform as democratizing the justice system.
laws.penalty: Judicial misconduct under new oversight tribunal: removal and disqualification. Electoral violations by judicial candidates: fines and disqualification.
exceptions: Some specialized courts (anti-corruption, electoral) have distinct selection mechanisms
Transitional provisions protect some existing judges through their terms

quiz.q: What made Mexico's 2024 judicial reform unprecedented worldwide?
options: It created a separate constitutional court for the first time
It made Mexico the first country to elect all federal judges by popular vote
It abolished judicial review of executive actions
It merged the judicial and legislative branches
quiz.explanation: Mexico became the first country in the world to require the election of all federal judges — including Supreme Court justices — by direct popular vote, raising significant rule-of-law concerns.

laws.title: First Judicial Elections Under 2024 Reform
laws.subtitle: Mexico held the world's first popular election for Supreme Court justices in 2025
laws.fullDescription: Following the passage of Mexico's controversial judicial reform in September 2024 — which required all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote — Mexico prepared for the world's first such election. The first judicial elections were scheduled for June 2025. Candidates had to pass a pre-screening process, but critics argued the process was politically influenced. The outgoing Supreme Court justices, whose terms were cut short by the reform, filed constitutional challenges. The US and Canada expressed concern about rule-of-law implications for USMCA. Major international law firms and multinational corporations began contingency planning for potential uncertainty in Mexico's legal system.
laws.penalty: Corruption by elected judges: enhanced penalties under new judicial oversight tribunal. Electioneering by judicial candidates beyond permitted campaign norms: disqualification.
exceptions: Existing commercial arbitration awards remain enforceable under USMCA regardless of domestic court changes
Specialized anti-corruption courts have different selection mechanism under transition provisions
laws.sourceLabel: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación

quiz.q: What made Mexico's June 2025 judicial elections historically unprecedented worldwide?
options: It was the first election where AI systems helped screen judicial candidates
It was the world's first popular election for Supreme Court justices
It was the first judicial election that included prosecutors as candidates
Mexico held elections for judges from 50 countries simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2025 judicial elections were the world's first instance of Supreme Court justices and federal judges being chosen by popular vote — no other country had implemented this system at the national level.

laws.title: Claudia Sheinbaum – Mexico's First Female President
laws.subtitle: Mexico elected its first female president — a climate scientist and former Mexico City mayor
laws.fullDescription: Claudia Sheinbaum won Mexico's June 2024 presidential election with 59% of the vote — the largest margin in Mexican democratic history — succeeding Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO) and becoming Mexico's first female president. Sheinbaum, a climate scientist and IPCC contributor, served as Mexico City's mayor. She pledged to continue AMLO's social programs while bringing greater technocratic competence and international engagement. Her administration committed to reducing violence, maintaining fiscal discipline, managing the USMCA relationship with the US amid concerns about Chinese investment in Mexico, and navigating the controversial judicial reform. She took office October 1, 2024.
laws.penalty: Electoral violations: up to 9 years imprisonment under COFIPE. Presidential authority under Article 89 of Mexican Constitution — emergency decree powers subject to constitutional limits.
exceptions: Presidential immunity during term for official acts
Opposition parties retain constitutional rights to campaign and hold office

quiz.q: What professional background distinguished Claudia Sheinbaum from most world leaders?
options: She was a retired military general before entering politics
She was a climate scientist who contributed to IPCC reports before becoming Mexico City mayor
She was a prominent human rights lawyer who prosecuted drug cartel members
She was a Nobel Prize-winning economist
quiz.explanation: Sheinbaum is a climate scientist with a PhD in energy engineering who contributed to the IPCC reports that won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007 — a background in climate science that is highly unusual among world leaders and shaped her policy positions.

laws.title: Mexico's 2024 Constitutional Judicial Reform
laws.subtitle: Popular election of Supreme Court judges creates unprecedented change
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's sweeping judicial reform (approved September 2024) under outgoing President López Obrador and continuing under President Claudia Sheinbaum will require popular election of all federal judges, including the Supreme Court justices. This makes Mexico the first country in the world to elect its Supreme Court by popular vote (the US elects state judges in some states). The reform passed over fierce opposition from judges, lawyers, and international observers including the US government and World Bank. All current Supreme Court justices must resign and stand for election or leave office.
laws.penalty: Judges who do not participate in the transition process: removal from office. Conduct unbecoming of a judge: now subject to politically-influenced judicial accountability bodies. Campaign finance violations in judicial elections: fines and disqualification
exceptions: Lower court judges have a staggered timeline for transitioning to elections
Military judges and administrative tribunals operate under separate systems
International arbitration panels operating in Mexico are not affected

quiz.q: What makes Mexico's 2024 judicial reform historically unprecedented?
options: It abolished the Supreme Court entirely
Mexico became the first country requiring popular election of all federal judges including Supreme Court
It reduced the number of Supreme Court justices from 11 to 5
It gave the president power to appoint all judges
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 judicial reform requires all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote — making Mexico the first country in the world to elect its highest court by direct national election.

laws.title: Mexico's Sheinbaum Government and Security Strategy
laws.subtitle: First female president inherits security crisis and judicial reform
laws.fullDescription: Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first female president on October 1, 2024, winning with 59% in a landslide. She inherited her predecessor López Obrador's controversial security strategy (hugs not bullets / 'abrazos no balazos'), the contentious judicial reform making judges elected, and an organized crime landscape. Sheinbaum began with a 'Plan México' to address insecurity through community development alongside security operations. Cartel violence continued in Sinaloa following the Culiacán War (after the arrest of Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada). Military deployments continue under expanded roles begun under AMLO.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking in Mexico: up to 40 years imprisonment. Cartel membership: up to 25 years. Money laundering: up to 15 years. Femicide: up to 60 years imprisonment (the highest sentence in Mexican law). Human trafficking: up to 25 years
exceptions: Voluntary surrender to authorities may reduce sentence under negotiated terms
Cooperating witnesses receive reduced sentences under organized crime law
Security forces' actions covered by use of force regulations (subject to ongoing human rights scrutiny)

quiz.q: What was historic about Mexico's October 2024 presidential transition?
options: First time power changed between political parties
Mexico became a republic for the first time
Claudia Sheinbaum became Mexico's first female president
The first President born outside Mexico City
quiz.explanation: Claudia Sheinbaum's inauguration on October 1, 2024 made her Mexico's first female president — a historic milestone for Latin America's second-largest economy, achieved by winning 59% of the vote in Mexico's most decisive electoral victory in decades.

laws.title: Femicide Laws and Gender-Based Violence Protections
laws.subtitle: Mexico classifies femicide as a distinct crime with enhanced penalties
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Federal Criminal Code and state criminal codes classify femicide (murder of a woman because of her gender) as a distinct and more severely punished crime than homicide. The law was strengthened following massive feminist protests in 2020. Femicide carries 40–70 years imprisonment at the federal level. However, enforcement and prosecution remain inconsistent, with many cases misclassified as suicides or accidents. Mexico also has an Emergency Alert System for Gender Violence that can be activated in states with high rates. Women's shelters (refugios) are protected spaces with strict legal privacy protections.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 40–70 years imprisonment; aggravated cases (involving public servants): life imprisonment
exceptions: Cases where gender motivation cannot be proven are classified as homicide
Procedural requirements for femicide classification vary by state

quiz.q: When did major feminist protests in Mexico push for stronger femicide laws?
quiz.explanation: Massive feminist protests in Mexico in 2020 led to strengthened femicide laws and greater government accountability for gender-based violence.

laws.title: Judicial Reform Controversy and Constitutional Amendment
laws.subtitle: Mexico's 2024 judicial reform eliminated appointment of judges by judicial councils
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's sweeping 2024 judicial reform, pushed through by outgoing President López Obrador, eliminated the independent judicial appointment system and replaced it with direct popular election of Supreme Court justices and all federal judges. The reform was deeply controversial: bar associations, legal scholars, and the US government raised concerns that it would undermine judicial independence and rule of law. Judges went on strike in protest. The reform also abolished the National Judicial Council, replacing it with a new body under greater executive influence. Incoming President Claudia Sheinbaum took office amid the legal upheaval. Foreign investment concerns about contract enforcement mounted.
laws.penalty: Not directly penal — restructures appointment of judiciary; electoral violations in new judicial elections subject to electoral court oversight
exceptions: Some transitional court compositions maintained during transition period
International arbitration tribunals operate separately from domestic courts
laws.sourceLabel: Mexico Diario Oficial de la Federacion

quiz.q: What unprecedented change did Mexico's 2024 judicial reform make to the selection of judges?
options: Judges chosen by direct popular election
Judges selected by professional bar associations
All judges appointed by the president
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 judicial reform introduced direct popular election of Supreme Court justices and all federal judges — an unprecedented change that critics argued would undermine judicial independence by making judges subject to political campaigns.

laws.title: Energy Sector Renationalization and PEMEX Reforms
laws.subtitle: Mexico reversed private energy investment under López Obrador and Sheinbaum
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's López Obrador government reversed many private energy sector reforms enacted under Peña Nieto by strengthening PEMEX (state oil company) and CFE (state power utility) positions in the energy market. Constitutional reforms prioritized state enterprises over private and foreign competitors in power dispatch and fuel contracts. International arbitration cases were filed by foreign energy investors claiming violations of USMCA investment protection provisions. The Sheinbaum government continued prioritizing state energy companies while also pursuing renewable energy investments through state entities. Mexico's energy legal framework remains highly politicized, with significant uncertainty for private investors.
laws.penalty: Violation of PEMEX fuel exclusivity provisions: contract cancellation; operating electricity generation without proper dispatch priority compliance: regulatory penalties
exceptions: Self-supply and generation for own use retain more flexibility
Industrial parks with on-site generation under transitional rules

quiz.q: What trade agreement have foreign energy investors used to file arbitration cases against Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Foreign energy investors have filed international arbitration cases against Mexico under USMCA (US-Mexico-Canada Agreement) investment protection provisions, arguing Mexico's energy renationalization policies violated their investment treaty rights.

laws.title: Mexico Fintech Law and Open Banking
laws.subtitle: Mexico's fintech law mandates open banking data sharing
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Fintech Law (2018) was Latin America's first comprehensive fintech regulation and includes provisions for open banking that require financial institutions to share customer data with authorized third parties when customers consent. The CNBV (banking regulator) has since issued secondary regulations on APIs, cybersecurity requirements for fintech firms, and anti-money laundering obligations specific to digital financial services.
laws.penalty: Fines and license revocation for non-compliant fintech firms; criminal penalties for fraud
exceptions: Traditional banks operating legacy systems during transition
Cooperative financial entities below thresholds
Academic fintech research

quiz.q: What was Mexico's Fintech Law notable for in Latin America?
options: First comprehensive fintech regulation in the region
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2018 Fintech Law was the first comprehensive fintech regulation in Latin America, including open banking mandates and AML requirements for digital financial services.

laws.title: Mexico Constitutional Energy Reform and Pemex Support
laws.subtitle: Mexico strengthens state role in energy under AMLO and Sheinbaum
laws.fullDescription: Mexico under Lopez Obrador (AMLO) and his successor Claudia Sheinbaum has maintained a strong state-centric approach to energy policy. Constitutional amendments strengthened the role of PEMEX (state oil company) and the CFE (state electricity company) over private renewable energy companies. The electricity reform gave priority to CFE power over private generators in dispatch order. Mexico has faced WTO challenges and disputes with trading partners under USMCA over these policies.
laws.penalty: Private generators who do not comply with CFE priority dispatch rules face contract penalties; disputes resolved through USMCA trade panels
exceptions: Self-supply electricity generation for own use
Communities generating small amounts of renewable power
Industrial facilities in special economic zones

quiz.q: What did Mexico's electricity reform give priority to in the power dispatch order?
options: CFE (state electricity company) power over private generators
quiz.explanation: Mexico's electricity reform gave dispatch priority to CFE-generated power over private renewable energy generators, a policy that drew WTO and USMCA trade challenges from the US and Canada.

laws.title: Mexico Judicial Election Reform
laws.subtitle: Mexico becomes first country to directly elect all federal judges
laws.fullDescription: President Claudia Sheinbaum enacted a landmark constitutional reform making Mexico the first country in the world to elect all federal judges by popular vote, including Supreme Court justices. The reform eliminated the existing federal judiciary and created a new one with elected judges serving 9-year terms. Critics including the US government, legal experts, and bar associations warned the reform would undermine judicial independence and make courts susceptible to political and organized crime influence. The reform passed in September 2024.
laws.penalty: The reform changes judicial selection procedures; violations of judicial conduct by elected judges face impeachment procedures
exceptions: State judiciary reforms are separate processes
Military courts retain their existing structure
Electoral tribunal continues under modified rules

quiz.q: What made Mexico's 2024 judicial reform a world first?
options: Creating the first supreme court in Latin America
Making Mexico the first country to elect all federal judges by popular vote
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 constitutional reform made it the first country in the world to require all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote rather than appointed.

laws.title: Plan C Judicial Reform
laws.subtitle: Mexico's sweeping overhaul of the federal judiciary
laws.fullDescription: Mexico passed a landmark constitutional reform replacing the appointment-based federal judiciary with popular elections for judges, including Supreme Court justices. The reform eliminates the existing judicial career service and requires all sitting federal judges to run for election or vacate their posts. Critics argue it undermines judicial independence while supporters say it democratizes justice. International bodies and the United States raised concerns about rule of law implications.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with transition provisions could result in removal from judicial office
exceptions: Transitional provisions allow some judges to serve until election cycles complete
Local courts have separate timelines

quiz.q: What does Mexico's Plan C judicial reform require for federal judges?
options: Popular elections to obtain or keep their posts
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Plan C reform requires federal judges including Supreme Court justices to be elected by popular vote rather than appointed.

laws.title: Constitutional Energy Nationalization
laws.subtitle: Mexico's reforms prioritizing state control of oil and electricity
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's constitutional reforms under President AMLO prioritized state-owned PEMEX and CFE (electricity) over private and foreign energy investment. Amendments to the electricity law gave CFE priority grid access and limited private renewable energy development. The hydrocarbon law reduced contracting mechanisms available to private oil companies. These reforms were challenged under the USMCA trade agreement by the United States and Canada, arguing they violated investment protection commitments. The constitutional reform specifically passed in 2024 consolidated state energy dominance.
laws.penalty: Energy companies operating without proper CFE coordination face contract cancellation; PEMEX and CFE violations of their own mandate carry administrative penalties on state officers
exceptions: Existing private energy contracts maintain transitional protections
Self-supply electricity generation for own-use continues under modified rules
Renewable energy for export receives special consideration
laws.sourceLabel: Diario Oficial de la Federacion Mexico

quiz.q: Which international trade agreement did the US and Canada use to challenge Mexico's energy reforms?
quiz.explanation: The United States and Canada filed formal dispute mechanisms under the USMCA (the replacement for NAFTA) challenging Mexico's energy reforms as violations of investment protection and market access commitments in the trade agreement.

laws.title: GMO Corn and Glyphosate Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Mexico's ban on GM corn imports and phaseout of glyphosate
laws.fullDescription: Mexico issued decrees restricting the use of genetically modified corn for human consumption, favoring native corn varieties, and phasing out glyphosate herbicide. The restrictions reflected both health concerns and cultural attachment to native Mexican corn varieties central to the country's food heritage and indigenous cultures. The United States challenged Mexico's GM corn restrictions under the USMCA dispute mechanism, arguing they were not science-based and constituted a trade barrier. A USMCA panel issued a ruling partly supporting the US position regarding tortilla and masa corn specifically.
laws.penalty: Importing prohibited GM corn products for human consumption carries fines and product confiscation; using glyphosate in excess of permitted amounts carries agricultural license penalties
exceptions: GM corn for animal feed continues under modified rules
Research institutions can use GM corn under controlled conditions
Yellow corn primarily for industrial ethanol production has different treatment

quiz.q: Through what trade agreement mechanism did the US challenge Mexico's GM corn restrictions?
options: UN Food and Agriculture Organization mediation
quiz.explanation: The United States challenged Mexico's GM corn restrictions through the USMCA (United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement) dispute settlement mechanism, arguing the restrictions were not science-based and constituted an unjustified trade barrier.

laws.title: Judicial Reform Constitutional Amendment
laws.subtitle: Overhauling Mexico's federal judiciary with elected judges
laws.fullDescription: Mexico passed a sweeping constitutional reform in 2024 to make federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, subject to popular election rather than appointment. The reform, championed by President Claudia Sheinbaum's Morena party, replaces the existing merit-based appointment system with direct elections for thousands of judicial positions. Critics argue it undermines judicial independence; proponents say it democratizes justice.
laws.penalty: Judges who fail to comply with new certification and election requirements face removal from office. Transitional provisions require all sitting federal judges to stand for reelection or vacate.
exceptions: Local state judges remain under state jurisdiction rules
Administrative tribunal judges covered by separate legislation

quiz.q: What is the main change introduced by Mexico's 2024 judicial reform?
options: Making federal judges subject to popular election
quiz.explanation: The reform makes federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, subject to popular election rather than presidential appointment, a historic and controversial change to Mexico's judicial system.

laws.title: Mexico Water Scarcity Crisis and Monterrey Emergency
laws.subtitle: Extreme water rationing as northern cities face depletion
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's water crisis intensified in 2024–2025, with Monterrey (Mexico's second-largest industrial city, population 5 million) experiencing its second major water rationing crisis in years. The La Boca and Cerro Prieto reservoirs hit critical levels below 10% capacity. The federal government enacted emergency measures including rationing schedules (water available only every 2-3 days per zone), accelerated construction of new pipelines from distant sources, and legal restrictions on car washing and private pool filling during dry season.
laws.penalty: Commercial establishments using water for prohibited purposes during rationing emergency: fines of MXN 50,000–500,000. Agricultural water users exceeding allocated quotas during emergency: concession suspension.
exceptions: Hospitals and medical facilities receive priority continuous water supply
Food production facilities with critical cooling needs qualify for emergency waivers
Industrial users with closed water recycling systems not subject to rationing
laws.sourceLabel: CONAGUA - National Water Commission of Mexico

quiz.q: Below what reservoir capacity level did Monterrey's La Boca and Cerro Prieto reservoirs fall during Mexico's water crisis?
quiz.explanation: Monterrey's key reservoirs fell below 10% capacity during Mexico's 2024-2025 water crisis, triggering extreme rationing measures that provided water to some zones only every 2-3 days in Mexico's second-largest industrial city of 5 million people.

laws.title: Mexico Supreme Court Reform: Eliminating Plurinominal Seats
laws.subtitle: Sheinbaum government's judicial and legislative changes
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum administration, building on Morena's supermajority in Congress, enacted further constitutional changes in 2024–2025. These included eliminating the proportional representation (plurinominal) seats in Congress that had allowed minority party representation, reducing the Supreme Court from 11 to 9 justices with elected positions, and establishing new regulatory agencies under greater executive control. Critics argued these consolidated Morena's political dominance and weakened checks and balances.
laws.penalty: Judicial officials who apply the old appointment procedures after constitutional changes take effect face administrative disciplinary action. Legislators who obstruct constitutional reforms validly passed by supermajority face censure.
exceptions: Existing Supreme Court justices may serve out their current terms or apply under the new elected process
Congressional staff positions retain civil service protections regardless of political changes

quiz.q: What happened to Mexico's Supreme Court size under the Sheinbaum-era judicial reform?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's judicial reform reduced the Supreme Court from 11 to 9 justices under the Morena government's constitutional changes, while also making justices subject to popular election rather than appointment — part of broader changes critics said concentrated power in the ruling party.

laws.title: Electricity Sector Reform (Constitutional Amendment)
laws.subtitle: Re-nationalization of electricity generation and distribution
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's constitutional reform returned majority control of electricity generation to the state-owned CFE (Comisión Federal de Electricidad), reversing the 2013 energy liberalization. Private renewable energy contracts were subject to renegotiation, and the National Energy Control Center was transferred to CFE. The reform sparked international arbitration from foreign investors.
laws.penalty: Private operators generating electricity without CFE partnership face license revocation and fines
exceptions: Small-scale rooftop solar for self-consumption
Existing grandfathered legacy contracts

quiz.q: What does CFE stand for in Mexico's electricity sector?
quiz.explanation: CFE stands for Comisión Federal de Electricidad, Mexico's state-owned electricity utility that was given majority control of generation under the reform.

laws.title: Judicial Reform: Elected Judges and Supreme Court Reduction
laws.subtitle: Mexico's constitutional reform to elect judges by popular vote
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted a landmark constitutional reform under President Claudia Sheinbaum requiring federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be elected by popular vote rather than appointed. The Supreme Court was reduced from 11 to 9 justices. The reform was highly controversial, with critics arguing it would politicise the judiciary and undermine rule of law. The US expressed concerns about its impact on trade and investment under USMCA.
laws.penalty: Judicial officers not participating in the transition elections face removal from office
exceptions: Administrative tribunal members follow separate transition procedures
Local state court judges subject to state-level implementation timelines

quiz.q: Under Mexico's 2024 judicial reform, how are federal judges selected?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's landmark 2024 constitutional reform replaced the appointment system with popular elections for federal judges including Supreme Court justices — a first among major democracies.

laws.title: Renewable Energy Auction Revival and Grid Modernisation
laws.subtitle: Mexico restores competitive renewables bidding under new government
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's new government under Claudia Sheinbaum reversed earlier CFE monopoly-expansion policies and revived competitive auctions for renewable energy projects. Grid modernisation legislation required CENACE (National Energy Control Center) to prioritise renewable dispatch and created investment frameworks for private renewable developers to participate alongside CFE. Mexico targeted 40% clean energy by 2035.
laws.penalty: Renewable developers not meeting environmental mitigation plans: permit suspension; grid operators prioritising fossil fuels over dispatched renewables: regulatory sanctions
exceptions: CFE-built renewable projects exempt from some auction competitive requirements
Emergency grid stability orders can temporarily override renewable dispatch priority

quiz.q: What is Mexico's clean energy target for 2035 under the new government's policy?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Sheinbaum government set a target of 40% clean energy by 2035, reviving the renewable energy auction system that had been largely frozen under the previous administration's CFE-first policy.

laws.title: Train Maya Environmental Impact and Indigenous Consultation
laws.subtitle: Mexico's controversial tourist railway through the Yucatan faces legal challenges
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Tren Maya project — a 1,500 km tourist railway through the Yucatan Peninsula — faced ongoing legal challenges over inadequate indigenous consultation and environmental impacts on the Maya Biosphere. Courts issued temporary injunctions over sections passing through protected jungle areas. The government enacted emergency decrees to protect the project's completion, creating a constitutional conflict over indigenous rights.
laws.penalty: Construction crews violating injunction orders: contempt of court proceedings; indigenous community members blocking construction: criminal trespass charges
exceptions: Already-completed sections continue operations regardless of pending litigation
Archaeological discoveries during construction trigger mandatory INAH review process

quiz.q: What type of rights did the Tren Maya project face challenges over failing to respect?
options: Indigenous consultation rights under Mexican law and ILO Convention 169
quiz.explanation: The Tren Maya faced repeated legal challenges over inadequate prior consultation with indigenous Maya communities, as required under Mexico's constitution and ILO Convention 169 — the international standard for consulting indigenous peoples about projects on their lands.

laws.title: Mexico Judicial Reform and Constitutional Transformation
laws.subtitle: Popular election of judges and court restructuring
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Constitutional Reform of 2024-2025, passed under President Claudia Sheinbaum's continuation of the MORENA agenda, enacted the most sweeping judicial transformation in Mexican history. The reform replaces appointment of Supreme Court justices and federal judges with direct popular election, reduces the Supreme Court from 11 to 9 justices, abolishes the Federal Judiciary Council, creates a new Judicial Discipline Tribunal, and establishes an Electoral Court with judges also elected by popular vote. The US and Canadian governments expressed concern about judicial independence under USMCA, while international legal organizations criticized the reform as threatening rule of law.
laws.penalty: Electoral campaign violations for judicial candidates: 15 years disqualification; judicial conduct violations: removal by Judicial Discipline Tribunal; judicial corruption: 20 years imprisonment under newly expanded criminal codes
exceptions: Specialized courts for organized crime (CENAPI) maintain appointment rather than election system
Military courts maintain separate constitutional structure
Administrative courts below federal level retain existing appointment mechanisms

quiz.q: What major change did Mexico's 2024-2025 judicial reform make to how Supreme Court justices are selected?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's landmark judicial reform replaced the appointment system with direct popular election of Supreme Court justices and federal judges — a controversial change that drew significant international concern about judicial independence.

laws.title: Mexico Constitutional Transformation and Sheinbaum Administration
laws.subtitle: Continuing MORENA's structural reforms
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted the Second Constitutional Transformation Implementation Act 2025 under President Claudia Sheinbaum, continuing the MORENA movement's agenda. The law implements the healthcare universalization plan establishing the Instituto Mexicano para la Atención a la Salud (IMAS) to replace IMSS-Bienestar, codifies the Sembrando Vida and Becas Bienestar social programs as constitutional rights, introduces the Plan México industrial policy prioritizing domestic production of pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, creates the National Women's Security Programme with dedicated infrastructure and protocols for femicide prevention, and establishes Sheinbaum's signature 'Clinic on Wheels' programme providing mobile health services to rural communities.
laws.penalty: IMAS service denial based on non-coverage status: administrative sanction plus criminal referral; social program fraud: 10 years imprisonment; femicide protocol non-compliance by prosecutors: career sanction
exceptions: Private healthcare providers not receiving public funding retain full operational autonomy
Religious organizations may decline specific services conflicting with doctrine
Emergency healthcare services must be provided regardless of insurance status

quiz.q: What new healthcare institution does Mexico's 2025 Constitutional Transformation Act create to universalize health services?
options: IMAS (Instituto Mexicano para la Atención a la Salud)
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2025 Constitutional Transformation Act creates IMAS (Instituto Mexicano para la Atención a la Salud) — a new universal healthcare institution designed to provide health services to all Mexicans regardless of employment or insurance status.

laws.title: Mexico National Guard Militarization and Public Security Act
laws.subtitle: Military permanently replacing civilian police
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted the National Guard Constitutional Integration and Security Militarization Act 2025, completing the Sheinbaum government's integration of the National Guard into the Secretariat of National Defence (SEDENA). The constitutional amendment permanently placed the National Guard under military command, authorized troops to conduct law enforcement operations without civilian judicial oversight in designated security emergency zones, created a military security court system for organized crime cases, established the Joint Security Intelligence Command combining CISEN intelligence and military intelligence, and expanded military authority over ports, airports, and border crossings. Critics warned of unprecedented civilian-military power concentration; proponents cited declining homicide rates in military-secured zones.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of National Guard operations: 15 years imprisonment; organized crime membership: 40 years; military intelligence obstruction: 25 years; arms trafficking to cartels: life imprisonment
exceptions: Military operations remain bound by international humanitarian law in civilian areas
Diplomatic and consular premises retain conventional security arrangements
Emergency evacuation corridors during natural disasters have civilian coordination primacy

quiz.q: Under which Mexican government ministry is the National Guard permanently placed under the 2025 Militarization Act?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's National Guard Constitutional Integration Act permanently places the National Guard under the Secretariat of National Defence (SEDENA) — effectively militarizing Mexico's primary domestic security force and giving the military unprecedented authority over civilian law enforcement.

laws.title: Claudia Sheinbaum Judicial Reform and Controversy Act
laws.subtitle: Elected judiciary and constitutional super-majority transformation
laws.fullDescription: President Claudia Sheinbaum's government built on predecessor AMLO's judicial reform that controversially introduced popular elections for Supreme Court justices. New implementing legislation establishes the electoral framework for judicial elections, creates a new simplified federal court system replacing many tribunals, and restructures the National Guard under clear civilian oversight. Critics and the US government expressed concerns about the judicial reform's impact on rule of law and investor confidence.
laws.penalty: Judges who fail to comply with their electoral mandate disclosures face disqualification. Attorneys who attempt to bribe elected judges face enhanced penalties under new judicial independence provisions.
exceptions: Specialized intellectual property and trade courts retain appointment rather than election processes
International arbitration panels operating under USMCA retain their existing frameworks

quiz.q: What unprecedented change to the judiciary did Mexico introduce under AMLO that Sheinbaum's government implemented?
options: Popular elections for Supreme Court justices
quiz.explanation: Mexico controversially introduced popular elections for Supreme Court justices — an unprecedented reform that critics argued would politicize the judiciary and undermine judicial independence.

laws.title: Judicial Election Implementation and Court Independence Act
laws.subtitle: First elected Supreme Court transition
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted implementing legislation for its constitutional reform introducing judicial elections. The law governs the transition process for electing Supreme Court justices and federal judges, establishes campaign finance rules for judicial candidates, creates the independent electoral tribunal for judicial races, and sets qualifications requirements for candidates. The first judicial elections took place in June 2025 under this framework.
laws.penalty: Judicial candidates who receive undisclosed campaign donations face disqualification. Judges who campaign on specific case outcomes face removal. Interference with judicial electoral processes carries up to eight years.
exceptions: Sitting judges who choose not to participate in the election process may retire with full pension benefits rather than face electoral removal
Specialist courts in complex technical areas may retain modified appointment procedures

quiz.q: When did Mexico's first judicial elections take place under the new framework?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's first judicial elections — a historic and globally unprecedented step — took place in June 2025, allowing ordinary citizens to vote for Supreme Court justices and federal judges for the first time.

laws.title: Femicide and Gender Violence Emergency Prevention Act
laws.subtitle: Addressing Mexico's epidemic of violence against women
laws.fullDescription: Mexico enacted emergency legislation in response to persistently high rates of femicide (the murder of women because of their gender). The law creates a national femicide alert system with real-time tracking, mandates specialized prosecutor units for gender violence in all states, establishes protective order enforcement mechanisms, creates economic independence programs for women in abusive relationships, and establishes clear definitions and enhanced penalties.
laws.penalty: Femicide carries 40-60 years imprisonment with no possibility of parole. Intimate partner murder with gender motivation is automatically classified as femicide. Officials who fail to properly investigate gender violence complaints face up to three years.
exceptions: Self-defense claims in domestic violence contexts receive an enhanced presumption of reasonableness
Trafficking victims who committed crimes under coercion receive specialized consideration in prosecution

quiz.q: Approximately how many women are murdered in Mexico each day in femicides?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 10 women are murdered in Mexico each day in what are classified as femicides — murders motivated by the victim's gender. Mexico has one of the highest femicide rates in Latin America, prompting mass protests by women's groups.

laws.title: Mexico Judicial Reform and Election of Judges Act
laws.subtitle: Supreme Court Popular Election Law
laws.fullDescription: Implements Mexico's controversial constitutional reform to elect all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, by popular vote rather than appointment. The law establishes the Judicial Discipline Tribunal, replaces the Federal Judiciary Council, creates the framework for judicial elections beginning in 2025, and establishes candidate vetting processes. Critics including the U.S. government and legal scholars warned the reform could undermine judicial independence.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for judges violating campaign and electoral neutrality rules
exceptions: Local state judges follow separate state-level electoral rules
Temporary judges remain appointed pending full reform implementation

quiz.q: What does Mexico's Judicial Reform Act change about Supreme Court justices?
options: They are elected by popular vote
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Judicial Reform Act requires all federal judges including Supreme Court justices to be elected by popular vote.

laws.title: Mexico Water Crisis and National Water Plan Emergency Act
laws.subtitle: Drought Emergency and Aquifer Protection Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses Mexico's severe water crisis with northern cities including Monterrey running out of water. The law creates emergency water transfer authorities, mandates aquifer recharge programs, establishes water tariffs that fund infrastructure investment, prohibits new industrial water concessions in critically stressed basins, creates desalination plant construction programs for northern Mexico, and establishes water security as a national security priority.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for unauthorized aquifer extraction; fines up to MXN 10 million for industry violations
exceptions: Agricultural water rights under existing concessions have transition period
Emergency municipal water supply receives priority allocation

quiz.q: Which major Mexican city experienced running out of water, driving the Water Crisis Act?
quiz.explanation: Monterrey's severe water shortage — when the city nearly ran out of water — was a key driver of Mexico's National Water Plan Emergency Act.

laws.title: Mexico First Female President and Claudia Sheinbaum Governance Act
laws.subtitle: Morena Continuity and Climate Science Leadership Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes the governance priorities of President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico's first female president, continuing AMLO's Fourth Transformation. The law codifies the Mexico City climate plan nationally, creates the National Energy Transition Commission, maintains social welfare programs (Sembrando Vida, Becas Benito Juarez), establishes the National Guard as permanent security institution, and creates renewable energy expansion targets.
laws.penalty: Administrative accountability mechanisms for program implementation
exceptions: Security operations retain operational confidentiality
International treaty obligations maintained regardless of domestic law

quiz.q: What distinction does Claudia Sheinbaum hold in Mexican political history?
quiz.explanation: Claudia Sheinbaum, inaugurated in October 2024, is Mexico's first female president, a historic milestone in Mexican politics.

laws.title: Mexico National Reforestation and Sembrando Vida Environmental Act
laws.subtitle: Tree Planting and Rural Livelihood Program Law
laws.fullDescription: Expands Mexico's Sembrando Vida program that pays rural farmers to plant trees and practice sustainable agriculture. The law targets 1 billion trees planted by 2030, creates agroforestry payments for participating communities, establishes carbon sequestration certification for voluntary markets, creates biodiversity monitoring protocols, and integrates the program with watershed protection and water security goals.
laws.penalty: Program exclusion and clawback for participating farmers who clear planted areas
exceptions: Existing agricultural operations maintain their status
Emergency drought situations have modified harvesting provisions

quiz.q: How many trees does Mexico's Sembrando Vida Expansion target planting by 2030?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Sembrando Vida Expansion targets planting 1 billion trees by 2030 through payments to rural farming communities.

laws.title: Judicial Reform and Elected Judges Controversy
laws.subtitle: Claudia Sheinbaum Implements AMLO Judicial Overhaul
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's incoming President Claudia Sheinbaum implemented the controversial judicial reform passed by outgoing AMLO's supermajority, making federal judges including Supreme Court justices subject to popular election. Critics warned it would politicize the judiciary and undermine judicial independence. The US and Canada expressed concern about rule of law implications for USMCA.
laws.penalty: Existing judicial appointments terminated; new elected system implemented
exceptions: Transition period for implementation
Constitutional minimum qualifications for candidates

quiz.q: What controversial change did Mexico make to its judiciary?
options: Made federal judges subject to popular election
Gave the president power to fire judges
quiz.explanation: Mexico enacted a controversial judicial reform making federal judges including Supreme Court justices subject to popular election, raising judicial independence concerns.

laws.title: Nearshoring Boom and Manufacturing Investment
laws.subtitle: Mexico Benefits From US-China Trade Decoupling
laws.fullDescription: Mexico surpassed China to become the United States' largest trade partner in 2023, capitalizing on nearshoring as companies moved manufacturing closer to the US market. Major investments flowed into automotive, electronics, and semiconductor sectors. The USMCA provided the legal framework while infrastructure constraints in northern states created bottlenecks.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; investment regulatory compliance
exceptions: USMCA rules of origin requirements
Environmental impact assessment for industrial parks

quiz.q: What major milestone did Mexico achieve in US trade in 2023?
options: Surpassed China to become largest US trade partner
quiz.explanation: Mexico surpassed China to become the largest US trade partner in 2023, capitalizing on nearshoring trends as companies moved manufacturing closer to the American market.

laws.title: Sheinbaum Inauguration and First Female President
laws.subtitle: Mexico Elects First Woman as President
laws.fullDescription: Claudia Sheinbaum was inaugurated as Mexico's first female president in October 2024, winning the June 2024 election by a massive margin.
