A climate scientist and former Mexico City mayor, Sheinbaum represented continuity with AMLO's Morena movement while promising to address gender-based violence, security, and economic development.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; democratic election and transition
exceptions: Constitutional transition protocols
Judicial reform ongoing parallel process

quiz.q: What profession is Claudia Sheinbaum trained in?
quiz.explanation: Claudia Sheinbaum is a climate scientist who served as Mexico City mayor before winning the 2024 election to become Mexico's first female president.

laws.title: Labor Reform and Independent Union Rights
laws.subtitle: Mexico's Historic Labor Democracy Changes
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's labor reform implemented as part of the USMCA agreement required workers to ratify collective bargaining agreements through genuine secret ballot elections, replacing the system of employer-controlled company unions. Independent unions grew rapidly, winning significant wage increases in manufacturing and automotive sectors.
laws.penalty: Fines for employers interfering with free union elections
exceptions: Small business thresholds
Agricultural sector different framework

quiz.q: What did Mexico's USMCA labor reform require for collective bargaining agreements?
options: Worker ratification through secret ballot elections
quiz.explanation: Mexico's USMCA labor reform required workers to ratify collective bargaining agreements through genuine secret ballot elections, replacing employer-controlled company union systems.

laws.title: Sargassum Crisis and Caribbean Tourism Impact
laws.subtitle: Mexico Battles Invasive Seaweed on Cancun Beaches
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Caribbean coast including Cancun and the Riviera Maya battled massive sargassum seaweed incursions that fouled beaches and impacted tourism. The government invested in barriers, removal equipment, and research into sargassum uses including fertilizer and biofuel. Climate change and Atlantic circulation changes drove increased sargassum blooms.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; beach management regulations
exceptions: Tourism business sargassum removal permits
Scientific collection permits

quiz.q: What causes the increasing sargassum seaweed on Mexico's Caribbean coast?
options: Atlantic circulation changes linked to climate change
quiz.explanation: Changes in Atlantic ocean circulation patterns linked to climate change drive massive sargassum seaweed blooms that foul Mexico's Caribbean beaches.

laws.title: Judicial Reform and Supreme Court Overhaul
laws.subtitle: Mexico elects judges by popular vote in historic constitutional change
laws.fullDescription: President Claudia Sheinbaum implemented a sweeping judicial reform that eliminated the professional appointment process for judges, replacing it with direct popular election of Supreme Court justices and other judges. The reform was deeply controversial, with the existing Supreme Court declaring it unconstitutional before being overruled. Critics argue elected judges will be politically influenced and lack technical expertise. The US expressed concern about rule of law implications. The reform is the most significant change to Mexico's judiciary since 1917.
laws.penalty: Sitting judges who did not participate in the transition process were removed from their positions
exceptions: Administrative and labor tribunals retained separate appointment process
Lower court judges have phased election schedule over several years

laws.title: Nearshoring Boom and Manufacturing Corridor Growth
laws.subtitle: Mexico captures manufacturing investment as companies leave China
laws.fullDescription: Mexico is the primary nearshoring beneficiary as US companies bring manufacturing closer to home from China. The Bajío region (Guadalajara, Querétaro, Aguascalientes, León) has become a major manufacturing corridor for electronics, automotive, and aerospace. Foreign direct investment hit record highs. Mexico surpassed China as the US's top trading partner in 2023. The USMCA trade agreement provides preferential access. Challenges include infrastructure bottlenecks, electricity supply constraints, and security concerns in some regions.
laws.penalty: Foreign companies must meet USMCA rules of origin requirements for preferential tariff treatment
exceptions: Maquiladora export processing zones have special customs treatment for imported inputs
Companies in special economic zones receive additional incentives beyond standard USMCA

quiz.q: When did Mexico overtake China as the United States' top trading partner?
quiz.explanation: Mexico surpassed China as the US's largest trading partner in 2023, driven by nearshoring as US companies relocated manufacturing closer to home amid supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions.

laws.title: Water Crisis in Mexico City and Megacity Scarcity
laws.subtitle: Mexico City faces Day Zero as aquifer sinks and pipes crumble
laws.fullDescription: Mexico City faces an existential water crisis. The city of 22 million sits on a former lake bed that is sinking as aquifers are depleted — some areas by 50cm per year. Half the piped water is lost to leaks. In 2024, the city faced 'Day Zero' fears as reservoirs hit record lows. Wealthy neighborhoods have private water trucks while poor communities go weeks without tap water. Climate change is intensifying droughts while the sinking ground cracks infrastructure.
laws.penalty: Water-intensive industries must implement recycling programs and pay water use fees
exceptions: Emergency water supply operations exempt from standard permits during declared water emergencies
Indigenous communities with traditional water rights have prior claims over new industrial users

quiz.q: How much water is lost to leaks in Mexico City's piped water system?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 50% of Mexico City's piped water is lost to leaks in the city's aging, crumbling infrastructure — an extraordinary waste in a city simultaneously facing severe water scarcity.

laws.title: Judicial Independence Crisis and Constitutional Court Overhaul
laws.subtitle: Mexico's controversial judiciary reforms reshaping democracy
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum inherited a landmark but controversial constitutional reform passed in the final months of Andrés Manuel López Obrador's presidency: a judicial overhaul that eliminated the appointed federal judiciary and replaced it with elected judges, including Supreme Court justices to be chosen by popular vote. Critics argued the reform would politicize the judiciary, eliminate judicial independence, and undermine rule of law — potentially violating Mexico-US-Canada trade agreement provisions. US officials and business groups expressed concern about contract enforcement and investment protection. Judges staged protests and work stoppages against the reform. The reform also eliminated judicial review mechanisms that had served as checks on executive power. Mexico simultaneously faces challenges from cartel violence, near-shoring manufacturing boom as companies relocate supply chains from China, and managing US-Mexico relations on immigration, trade, and drug enforcement.
laws.penalty: Judicial reforms changed the judicial structure; within Mexico's new system, various laws carry their own penalties
exceptions: Some specialized courts retained appointment processes

quiz.q: What made Mexico's judicial reform controversial internationally?
options: It replaced appointed federal judges with popularly elected judges including Supreme Court justices
It merged state and federal courts
It required all judges to hold law degrees from Mexican universities only
quiz.explanation: Mexico's judicial reform replaced the appointed federal judiciary — including Supreme Court justices — with popularly elected judges, which critics argued would politicize the judiciary and undermine judicial independence and rule of law.

laws.title: Nearshoring Boom and Supply Chain Migration from China
laws.subtitle: Mexico benefiting enormously from US-China trade decoupling
laws.fullDescription: Mexico has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the US-China trade war and supply chain diversification trend, receiving massive foreign investment as companies seek manufacturing locations close to the US market. The USMCA (US-Mexico-Canada Agreement) provides preferential access to the US market for goods manufactured in Mexico. Foreign direct investment in Mexico has surged, with major investments in automotive (BMWexpanding, Gigafactory planned by Tesla), electronics, textiles, aerospace, and industrial manufacturing. The Bajío region and northern border states have seen particularly intense industrial development. The nearshoring boom has put pressure on Mexico's electricity grid, water resources, and talent pipeline. Mexico has also navigated tensions between its economic relationship with the US and maintaining economic ties with China.
laws.penalty: Labor law requirements including minimum wages and union rights apply to manufacturers; environmental permits required for industrial operations
exceptions: Free trade zone and industrial park operations have specific regulatory frameworks

quiz.q: What trade agreement provides preferential US market access for Mexican manufactured goods?
quiz.explanation: The USMCA (US-Mexico-Canada Agreement), which replaced NAFTA in 2020, provides preferential access to the US market for goods manufactured in Mexico — a major factor driving the nearshoring investment boom.

laws.title: Nearshoring Manufacturing Boom
laws.subtitle: Mexico capitalizes on US-China trade war relocations
laws.fullDescription: Mexico has become the top US trading partner overtaking China, fueled by nearshoring as companies relocate supply chains closer to US consumers. Monterrey, Guadalajara and Tijuana are experiencing manufacturing booms with semiconductor, automotive and electronics firms investing heavily. Labor costs remain competitive but infrastructure bottlenecks including electricity and water shortages threaten the boom's sustainability.
laws.penalty: Foreign investment incentive programs require minimum employment thresholds; tax breaks clawed back if jobs targets unmet
exceptions: Maquiladora duty-free zones offer enhanced incentives
Special economic zones in southern states provide additional benefits

quiz.q: Which manufacturing sector has most driven Mexico's nearshoring boom?
quiz.explanation: Automotive and electronics manufacturing have been the primary drivers of Mexico's nearshoring boom as companies shift supply chains from Asia.

laws.title: Sheinbaum Judicial Reform and Court Packing
laws.subtitle: Mexico's historic judiciary overhaul faces constitutional crisis
laws.fullDescription: President Claudia Sheinbaum, elected in June 2024 as Mexico's first female president, pursued her predecessor AMLO's controversial judicial reform requiring judges, including Supreme Court justices, to be directly elected by popular vote. The reform passed with MORENA's supermajority and took effect in 2025. Critics called it the end of judicial independence as elected judges would be beholden to populist pressure. The US expressed concern about rule of law for trade under USMCA. Several Supreme Court justices resigned rather than stand for election.
laws.penalty: Judicial election process established; judges failing to file candidacy must leave their positions
exceptions: Transition period allows existing judges to serve until election cycle
Some specialized courts have different transition timelines

quiz.q: What unprecedented requirement did Mexico's 2024 judicial reform impose on Supreme Court justices?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2024 judicial reform required Supreme Court justices and other judges to be directly elected by popular vote, a requirement critics called the end of judicial independence as judges would face populist pressure.

laws.title: Starlink Rural Connectivity
laws.subtitle: Satellite internet transforms remote Mexican communities
laws.fullDescription: SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service has brought high-speed internet to remote Mexican communities that traditional infrastructure never reached. Mexico's mountainous terrain, Indigenous communities in remote areas and rural dispersal made conventional broadband deployment uneconomical. Starlink has been particularly impactful in Oaxaca, Chiapas and other states with large Indigenous populations. The service has enabled telemedicine, remote education and economic participation in communities previously digitally isolated. Mexico has also developed its own satellite program with mixed results.
laws.penalty: Satellite internet services require IFETEL spectrum authorization; unauthorized satellite operations subject to fines
exceptions: Personal residential Starlink terminals require simpler registration than commercial providers
Government-subsidized connectivity programs in remote areas have different pricing

quiz.q: Which mountainous Mexican states have most benefited from Starlink satellite internet connectivity?
quiz.explanation: Oaxaca and Chiapas, with their mountainous terrain and large Indigenous populations in remote communities, have most significantly benefited from Starlink satellite internet that reached areas where conventional broadband infrastructure was never economically viable.

laws.title: Pemex Debt Crisis and Energy Dependence
laws.subtitle: State oil company drowns in debt while Mexico imports refined products
laws.fullDescription: Pemex, Mexico's state oil company, is one of the world's most indebted companies with over $100 billion in debt. Production has declined for two decades from a peak of 3.4 million barrels per day to under 2 million. Despite being an oil producer, Mexico imports significant refined petroleum products because its refineries are insufficient. The AMLO and Sheinbaum administrations have continued pouring money into Pemex and building a new refinery at Dos Bocas that has been plagued by delays and cost overruns.
laws.penalty: Pemex receives government transfers to service debt; energy contracts governed by hydrocarbons law
exceptions: Private investment allowed in upstream but Pemex retains preferential rights
Fuel pricing regulated to maintain affordability despite fiscal cost

quiz.q: Despite being an oil producer, why does Mexico import significant petroleum products?
quiz.explanation: Despite being an oil producer, Mexico imports significant refined petroleum products because its domestic refining capacity is insufficient—a paradox that the government has tried to address through building the new Dos Bocas refinery, with mixed results.

laws.title: General Climate Change Law
laws.subtitle: Net Zero by 2050
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 2012 General Climate Change Law (LGCC) was among the first in the developing world to establish a comprehensive climate framework. The law sets targets of 30% emissions reduction by 2030 (compared to business-as-usual) and net zero by 2050. It created the National Emissions Registry (RENE) and a carbon trading scheme. Mexico ratified the Paris Agreement and updated its NDC, though critics note the Pemex-dominated energy sector and Lopez Obrador's support for fossil fuels undercut climate ambitions. The country faces severe droughts, increasing the urgency of adaptation.
laws.penalty: Administrative fines up to 300,000 days of minimum wage; environmental liability for damages
exceptions: Small enterprises below registration thresholds
Traditional indigenous land use

laws.title: Mexico Sugary Drink and Junk Food Tax
laws.subtitle: Fighting Latin America's Obesity Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Mexico implemented a pioneering sugar-sweetened beverage tax of 1 peso per liter in 2014, along with an 8% tax on high-calorie non-essential foods. Mexico has one of the world's highest rates of obesity and diabetes — over 70% of adults are overweight or obese, and diabetes is a leading cause of death. Research showed the soda tax reduced consumption by 5.5-12% in the first year, and the food tax reduced purchases of taxed items. Mexico also adopted front-of-pack warning labels (octagonal 'stop' signs) for foods high in sugar, sodium, fat, and calories.
laws.penalty: Tax levied on manufacturers and importers; customs enforcement for imported products
exceptions: Plain water and unflavored beverages
Products below caloric thresholds

laws.title: Mexico Labor Reform — Authentic Trade Unions
laws.subtitle: USMCA and Union Democracy
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 2019 Labor Reform, prompted by USMCA trade agreement requirements, fundamentally changed Mexican labor relations. Previously, 'ghost unions' (sindicatos charros) — employer-controlled unions that workers never voted for — dominated Mexican industry, suppressing wages. The reform requires all existing collective bargaining agreements to be renegotiated with worker votes, creates an independent Federal Center for Conciliation and Labor Registration, and mandates union democracy. Mexico's minimum wage has been raised dramatically — from $2.50/day to $13/day — with border zone workers receiving higher rates. The reform transformed Mexico's labor landscape.
laws.penalty: Unfair labor practices: STPS enforcement; employer interference in union elections: criminal liability; minimum wage violations: fines
exceptions: Seasonal agricultural workers under adapted provisions
Domestic workers have strengthened but distinct protections

laws.title: Mexico Free Compulsory Education and UNAM
laws.subtitle: Biggest University in the Americas
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Constitution mandates free, compulsory, secular education from preschool through upper secondary (preparatoria). The UNAM (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México) is the largest university in the Americas by enrollment (350,000+ students) and charges virtually no tuition. Mexico's rural education quality gap — between urban and rural schools, particularly for indigenous communities — is significant. Mexico implemented educational reforms in 2013 (requiring teacher evaluations) that triggered massive teacher protests, and then reversed them in 2019 under López Obrador, who favored the powerful CNTE teachers union.
laws.penalty: Private school registration required; teacher certification monitored; school feeding programs legally mandated
exceptions: Religious schools operate under registration requirements
Indigenous community schools (CONAFE) under different framework

laws.title: Migration Law and US Transit Agreement
laws.subtitle: Mexico's transformation from sending to transit and receiving country
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Migration Law (2011) established modern immigration enforcement mechanisms. Mexico has faced intense US pressure to enforce its southern border against migrants from Central America and beyond transiting to the United States. The 'Remain in Mexico' (MPP) and 'Title 42' policies pushed by the US made Mexico a waiting area for asylum seekers. Mexico has deported millions of Central Americans. Simultaneously, hundreds of thousands of Americans and Canadians live in Mexico as residents. Mexico also receives Venezuelan, Haitian, and Cuban migrants.
laws.penalty: Irregular migrants in Mexico can be detained up to 36 hours (extendable) and deported; human smuggling (coyote operations) carries 5-15 years imprisonment; employers of undocumented workers face fines
exceptions: Refugees and asylum seekers may apply to COMAR (Mexican refugee agency) for protection
MERCOSUR and certain treaty nationals have simplified entry

quiz.q: The 'Remain in Mexico' policy, officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols, required asylum seekers to wait in Mexico while their US cases were processed. Which administration implemented it?
quiz.explanation: The Remain in Mexico policy (Migrant Protection Protocols) was implemented by the first Trump administration in January 2019, requiring non-Mexican asylum seekers who crossed the US border to wait in Mexico during US immigration proceedings.

laws.title: Drug Decriminalization and Cartel War
laws.subtitle: Mexico's personal drug use decriminalization amid cartel violence
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's General Health Law decriminalized possession of small amounts of drugs for personal use (2009): up to 5g marijuana, 0.5g cocaine, 50mg heroin, 40mg methamphetamine. Mexico is a major transit country for cocaine (from Colombia) and the world's primary fentanyl producer (via Chinese precursor chemicals). The Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel) are among the world's most powerful criminal organizations. Mexico has suffered 30,000+ drug war-related murders annually since 2019. The Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled cannabis prohibition unconstitutional.
laws.penalty: Trafficking: 10-25 years (cartel members face enhanced sentences); production/cultivation: 10-25 years; personal use possession (above limits): 3-15 years; money laundering drug proceeds: 5-15 years; cartel leaders: extradited to US for prosecution
exceptions: Personal possession under specified limits decriminalized since 2009
Supreme Court rulings have created de facto cannabis legalization for adults in some jurisdictions
laws.sourceLabel: Mexico Ley General de Salud Art. 478-480 (Drug Policy)

quiz.q: Mexico is the world's primary source of which synthetic opioid that has caused mass casualties in the United States?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's cartels, primarily the Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG, produce the vast majority of fentanyl consumed in the United States, using chemical precursors sourced from China. This synthetic opioid is responsible for over 70,000 US overdose deaths annually.

laws.title: Same-Sex Marriage and LGBTQ+ Rights
laws.subtitle: Mexico's state-by-state LGBTQ+ progress
laws.fullDescription: Mexico has been advancing LGBTQ+ rights through Supreme Court rulings and state legislation. Mexico City legalized same-sex marriage in 2009 (first in Latin America outside Argentina). The Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that all states must recognize same-sex marriages from other states. By 2022, all 31 Mexican states and Mexico City had legalized same-sex marriage, either by law or court order. Mexico's Supreme Court has also recognized non-binary gender recognition. Mexico City has comprehensive LGBTQ+ anti-discrimination ordinances. Violence against LGBTQ+ individuals, particularly transgender women, remains high.
laws.penalty: LGBTQ+ discrimination by government entities or businesses: civil and administrative penalties under federal anti-discrimination law (CONAPRED); hate crimes: enhanced criminal penalties; conversion therapy: banned in Mexico City and several states
exceptions: Some states are slower to implement Supreme Court same-sex marriage mandates
Religious organizations retain exemptions in some contexts
Federal law provides baseline protections but state implementation varies

quiz.q: Mexico City's 2009 same-sex marriage legalization was historic because it was the first where in Latin America?
quiz.explanation: Mexico City's 2009 same-sex marriage law made it the first jurisdiction in Latin America to legalize same-sex marriage (Argentina had not yet legalized it nationally — Argentina did so in 2010). This was historic for the region and preceded by a year Argentina's national legalization.

laws.title: Most Dangerous Country for Journalists in the Americas
laws.subtitle: Mexico consistently leads the hemisphere in journalist murders due to organized crime
laws.fullDescription: Mexico is the most dangerous country in the Americas for journalists, with dozens murdered each year primarily by drug cartels. The constitution guarantees freedom of the press, but in practice journalists covering organized crime, corruption, and local politics face existential danger. The government mechanism FEADLE (Federal Mechanism for Protection of Human Rights Defenders and Journalists) provides inadequate protection. Impunity for journalist murders exceeds 99%. Self-censorship is widespread. Mexico ranks in the bottom third globally for press freedom according to RSF.
laws.penalty: No state censorship; criminal defamation laws exist; journalist murders face near-total impunity
exceptions: Federal protection mechanism exists but is widely considered ineffective
laws.sourceLabel: DOF - Diario Oficial de la Federación

quiz.q: What is the approximate impunity rate for journalist murders in Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Mexico has an impunity rate exceeding 99% for journalist murders — meaning fewer than 1% of journalist killings result in conviction. This near-total impunity makes Mexico the most dangerous country in the Americas for journalists.

laws.title: Digital Policy and LFPDPPP Data Protection
laws.subtitle: Mexico has federal data protection law but limited social media regulation
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Federal Law on Protection of Personal Data Held by Private Parties (LFPDPPP, 2010) governs how companies collect and use personal data. The National Institute for Transparency (INAI) enforces data protection. Mexico has been slower than the EU or Brazil to update its digital regulations, though reform discussions are ongoing. Social media is heavily used in Mexico, and platforms have been criticized for inadequate response to violence-related content. Content moderation challenges are acute in Mexico given the prevalence of organized crime using social media for recruitment and messaging. The Mexican government has used social media extensively for communications.
laws.penalty: LFPDPPP violations: fines up to 320,000 UMAs; INAI enforcement authority
exceptions: Law enforcement and national security have broad exemptions

quiz.q: What challenge does content moderation on social media face specifically in Mexico?
options: Government requests for opposition content removal
Organized crime using social media for recruitment and messaging
quiz.explanation: Mexico's most acute social media content moderation challenge is organized crime's extensive use of platforms for recruitment, messaging, and even showcasing violence — creating pressure on platforms that often don't effectively enforce their own policies against cartel-related content.

laws.title: Fintech Law and SPEI — Mexico's Digital Banking Revolution
laws.subtitle: Mexico's Fintech Law was Latin America's first comprehensive fintech regulatory framework
laws.fullDescription: Mexico passed the Fintech Law (Ley para Regular las Instituciones de Tecnología Financiera) in 2018 — Latin America's first comprehensive fintech regulatory framework, covering crowdfunding, e-money, and cryptocurrency institutions. CNBV (National Banking and Securities Commission) and Banxico (central bank) regulate financial institutions. Mexico's SPEI (Interbank Electronic Payment System) is the backbone of digital payments. Mexico launched CoDi (digital payment system) and later DiMo for mobile payments. Mexico has a large unbanked population that fintech is reaching. Mexico also faces significant challenges with cartel money laundering through the financial system.
laws.penalty: CNBV and Banxico regulatory enforcement; fintech licensing violations carry administrative penalties; AML violations subject to criminal prosecution
exceptions: Some small cooperative financial entities have simplified regulatory requirements

quiz.q: What distinction does Mexico's 2018 Fintech Law hold in Latin America?
options: The first country to launch a CBDC
Latin America's first comprehensive fintech regulatory framework
The strictest crypto ban in the region
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2018 Fintech Law was Latin America's first comprehensive regulatory framework for financial technology — covering crowdfunding platforms, electronic money institutions, and virtual asset services in a single law that became a model for other Latin American countries.

laws.title: COFEPRIS Food Regulation & Front-of-Pack Warning Labels
laws.subtitle: Mexico pioneered octagonal front-of-pack warning labels and strict junk food rules
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risk (COFEPRIS) regulates all food and beverages. Mexico was actually among the first countries globally to implement octagonal front-of-package warning labels (before Brazil), requiring bold black octagonal warnings on packaged food and beverages that exceed limits for calories, sugars, saturated fat, trans fat, and sodium — implemented in 2020 under NOM-051-SCFI/SSA1-2010 amendments. Mexico also introduced restrictions on advertising unhealthy food to children and banned the sale of such foods in schools. SENASICA (under SAGARPA/SADER) handles agricultural food safety, including Mexico's large fruit and vegetable export sector.
laws.penalty: COFEPRIS labeling violations: fines up to 20,000 times the daily minimum wage (~MXN 2 million+); selling food in violation of school prohibitions: fines and closure; adulterated food distribution: criminal charges
exceptions: Traditional artisanal foods (mezcal artesanal, queso Oaxaca) have modified production standards
Indigenous traditional food practices have cultural recognition exemptions
Small local producers below certain production thresholds have simplified registration

quiz.q: What global food policy innovation did Mexico implement in 2020 ahead of most other countries?
options: Front-of-pack octagonal black warning labels on unhealthy processed foods
Mandatory country of origin labeling on all imports
Blockchain tracking of all food imports
quiz.explanation: Mexico implemented its octagonal black front-of-package warning label system in 2020 under NOM-051, making it one of the world's first countries to require prominent warnings on foods exceeding limits for calories, sugars, saturated fat, trans fat, and sodium.

laws.title: Mexico Federal Animal Welfare Law and CDMX Bullfighting Ban
laws.subtitle: Mexico City de facto banned bullfighting in 2022
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Ley Federal de Sanidad Animal (Federal Animal Health Law) governs animal welfare at the national level, focusing on livestock but including some companion animal provisions. Mexico City's (CDMX) Ley de Protección a los Animales is the country's most comprehensive urban animal protection law. Mexico City was the first Mexican entity to effectively ban bullfighting when its Supreme Administrative Tribunal ruled in 2022 that bullfighting violated the city's animal protection law — a decision confirmed constitutionally. Street dog management uses trap-neuter-return (TNR) programs. Mexico also prohibits cockfighting in several states, though it remains legal in others.
laws.penalty: CDMX: fines from 20 to 500 days of minimum wage; up to 2 years imprisonment for aggravated cruelty; license revocations for businesses
exceptions: Livestock under NOM-033 federal standards
Scientific research with ethics committee approval
Traditional practices subject to ongoing legal dispute
Cockfighting legal in some states

quiz.q: What landmark animal welfare decision did Mexico City courts make regarding bullfighting in 2022?
options: They declared bullfighting a national heritage activity
They ruled bullfighting violated animal protection law, effectively banning it
They required veterinary supervision of all corridas
They mandated permits be renewed annually
quiz.explanation: Mexico City's Supreme Administrative Tribunal ruled in 2022 (confirmed constitutionally) that bullfighting contravened the city's animal protection law, effectively banning the practice in one of the world's largest cities.

laws.title: Mexico Family Law — Express Divorce and State Variation
laws.subtitle: Mexico City offers 'express divorce' and recognizes diverse family structures
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's family law varies significantly by state — the country has 31 state civil codes plus the Federal Civil Code. Mexico City (CDMX) has been at the forefront of reform: it legalized same-sex marriage in 2010 (the first jurisdiction in Latin America), introduced 'express divorce' (divorcio incausado) — an administrative divorce requiring no grounds and minimal process, and has the most progressive recognition of diverse family structures. Marriage in Mexico requires civil ceremony — only civil marriage is legally recognized (religious ceremonies alone have no legal effect). Mexico's Supreme Court has ruled that states denying same-sex marriage violate constitutional equality. Child custody (guarda y custodia) increasingly favors shared arrangements.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement through family courts; pension alimenticia (support) enforced by wage garnishment; civil arrest possible for willful non-support; criminal non-support charges in some states
exceptions: Premarital agreements (capitulaciones matrimoniales)
Separate property regimes available
Indigenous community customary law may apply in some circumstances
laws.sourceLabel: Mexico City Civil Code — Divorcio Incausado

quiz.q: What is the 'divorcio incausado' that Mexico City introduced as a family law innovation?
options: Administrative divorce requiring no stated grounds — express divorce without court showing cause
quiz.explanation: Mexico City's 'divorcio incausado' (no-fault or express divorce) allows either spouse to request divorce administratively without stating any grounds or fault — a streamlined process requiring minimal court involvement. This was a major access-to-justice reform that has been adopted by many Mexican states.

laws.title: Mexico Property Rights & Ejido Land System
laws.subtitle: Communal ejido land and private property framework
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's property system is shaped by the 1917 Revolution's ejido system — communal agricultural lands granted to rural communities — codified in the Ley Agraria (1992 reform). The 1992 reforms allowed ejidatarios to convert ejido land to private property for the first time. The Federal Civil Code governs urban private property. The government retains subsoil rights (including minerals and oil) constitutionally (Art. 27). Rent control was abolished in 1993, but Mexico City reintroduced some tenant protections through the CDMX Civil Code.
laws.penalty: Illegal occupation of ejido land: criminal liability; expropriation of private property requires prior compensation
exceptions: Subsoil resources belong to the nation, not landowners
Ejido conversion requires assembly vote of ejido members
laws.source: Constitucion Politica Art. 27; Ley Agraria; CCDF

quiz.q: Under Mexico's constitution, who owns subsoil resources like oil and minerals?
quiz.explanation: Article 27 of Mexico's Constitution establishes that subsoil resources — including oil, minerals, and hydrocarbons — belong to the nation, not private landowners, a principle stemming from the 1917 Revolution.

laws.title: Mexico PROFECO & Ley Federal de Proteccion al Consumidor
laws.subtitle: Federal consumer protection agency and rights
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Ley Federal de Proteccion al Consumidor (LFPC, 1992) governs consumer rights and established PROFECO (Procuraduria Federal del Consumidor) as the enforcement agency. PROFECO operates CONCILIANET for online dispute resolution, publishes 'quien es quien en los precios' (who's who in prices) for price comparison, and conducts market inspections. Consumers have a 5-day cancellation right for distance sales. The ley also requires suppliers to post prices in Mexican pesos (no dollar pricing in stores). E-commerce protections were strengthened via NOM-051 amendments. PROFECO can impose fines and order product recalls.
laws.penalty: LFPC violation: fines from MXN 500 to 5 million; product recall orders; temporary business closure
exceptions: 5-day cancellation right for distance sales
Prices must be shown in Mexican pesos in consumer contexts

quiz.q: What unique price transparency tool does Mexico's PROFECO publish to help consumers compare prices?
options: 'Quien es quien en los precios' (who's who in prices) comparison guide
quiz.explanation: PROFECO's 'Quien es quien en los precios' (who's who in prices) is a regular publication comparing prices of basic consumer goods across major retailers, helping Mexican consumers identify price gouging and find the best value — a transparency initiative unique in the Americas.

laws.title: Amparo — Constitutional Protection
laws.subtitle: Juicio de Amparo — Mexico's unique constitutional remedy
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Juicio de Amparo is a distinctive constitutional remedy allowing individuals to challenge government acts that violate constitutional rights, including laws themselves. It can be filed against any authority — federal, state, or municipal. A successful amparo suspends the challenged act. The amparo system is considered Mexico's most important legal institution, equivalent to a combined habeas corpus, injunction, and constitutional review. The 2011 constitutional reform expanded amparo to include international human rights treaties.
laws.penalty: Failing to comply with an amparo order: criminal contempt (desacato), removal from office. Judges who fail to grant valid amparos face discipline.
exceptions: Amparo effects are relative (only binding on parties — not erga omnes) except for constitutional jurisprudencia
Electoral matters excluded from amparo
Certain tax amparos have special suspension requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación

quiz.q: What makes Mexico's Juicio de Amparo unique compared to constitutional remedies in other countries?
options: It requires a jury of 12 citizens
It can challenge any government act violating constitutional rights — including laws themselves
It only applies to federal law violations
It requires Supreme Court approval before filing
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Juicio de Amparo can be filed against any government act — laws, regulations, judicial decisions, or administrative actions — that violates constitutional rights. This broad scope, combined with its suspension power, makes it Mexico's most powerful legal tool. The 2011 reform extended it to cover international human rights treaties.

laws.title: PEMEX & Energy Reform — Oil Nationalization
laws.subtitle: 1938 expropriation and 2013-2024 reform reversals
laws.fullDescription: Mexico nationalized its oil industry in 1938 under President Cárdenas, creating PEMEX (Petróleos Mexicanos). This was a defining moment of Mexican nationalism — March 18 is Oil Expropriation Day. The 2013 energy reform under Peña Nieto opened oil to private investment for the first time. President AMLO reversed this: the 2021 electricity reform restored CFE (state electricity company) priority, and 2022 reforms ended new private oil contracts. PEMEX is heavily indebted (~$100 billion) and receives massive government bailouts.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized oil/gas extraction: criminal prosecution. Energy sector violations: CRE (Energy Regulatory Commission) fines.
exceptions: Existing private contracts from 2013 reform remain valid for their duration
Foreign companies may partner with PEMEX under association agreements
Natural gas imports remain partially privatized

quiz.q: On what date does Mexico celebrate the anniversary of the 1938 oil nationalization?
quiz.explanation: Mexico celebrates March 18 as Oil Expropriation Day (Día de la Expropiación Petrolera), commemorating President Lázaro Cárdenas's 1938 nationalization of the oil industry and creation of PEMEX. The nationalization is considered one of Mexico's defining acts of economic sovereignty.

laws.title: TLCAN/USMCA — Agricultural Provisions
laws.subtitle: Trade agreement impacts on Mexican corn and farmers
laws.fullDescription: The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA/TLCAN, 1994) and its successor USMCA (T-MEC, 2020) have profoundly affected Mexican agriculture. US corn exports undercut Mexican small farmers (campesinos), displacing millions and contributing to migration. Mexican corn varieties — corn originated in Mexico — faced competition from subsidized US corn. Mexico has resisted GMO corn imports on cultural and environmental grounds. The 2023 GMO corn decree by AMLO became a trade dispute. USMCA's agricultural provisions require dispute resolution panels for such conflicts.
laws.penalty: USMCA violations: dispute panel proceedings, trade sanctions if findings adverse.
exceptions: Cultural foods (native corn varieties) may have heritage protections
Small subsistence farmers have social program support
Bio-safety rules may restrict GMO imports under Mexican law

quiz.q: What agricultural product from Mexico, the country of its origin, faced displacement from US imports after NAFTA?
quiz.explanation: Mexico is the birthplace of corn (maize), but NAFTA (1994) allowed heavily subsidized US corn to flood Mexican markets, undercutting small Mexican farmers (campesinos). This contributed to rural displacement and migration. Mexico has since resisted GMO corn imports, citing cultural heritage and environmental concerns about contaminating native varieties.

laws.title: Ley Migratoria — Migration & Central American Transit
laws.subtitle: Ley de Migración (2011) — Mexico as transit country
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Ley de Migración (2011) established rights for migrants and refugees while creating enforcement mechanisms. Mexico is both a destination and major transit country for Central American migrants heading to the US. Mexico implemented 'Migrant Protection Protocols' (Remain in Mexico) under US pressure (2019). The National Guard was deployed to southern borders. The Clandestine Migration Prevention Group (BETA) provides humanitarian assistance to migrants. Mexico hosts over 150,000 recognized refugees.
laws.penalty: Irregular entry: administrative detention, deportation. Smuggling migrants: 6-12 years imprisonment.
exceptions: UNHCR-recognized refugees may regularize status
Children cannot be detained in migration facilities
Humanitarian visa available for Central American migrants with certain vulnerabilities

quiz.q: What is Mexico's role in the Central American migration corridor?
options: Only accepts migrants under formal refugee procedures
quiz.explanation: Mexico serves as both a major transit country (for migrants from Central America and beyond heading to the US) and a destination country. Mexico has received significant US pressure to enforce its southern border and has deployed the National Guard there, while also hosting over 150,000 recognized refugees.

laws.title: Ley General del Equilibrio Ecológico — LGEEPA
laws.subtitle: Environmental protection framework — Areas Naturales Protegidas
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's LGEEPA (Ley General del Equilibrio Ecológico y la Protección al Ambiente, 1988) is the framework environmental law. It established the national system of protected natural areas (ANP), which covers 90+ million hectares (~17% of national territory). SEMARNAT enforces environmental regulations. Mexico is a megadiverse country — 10% of all species on Earth are found in Mexico. Key protected areas include the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, Sea of Cortez, and Calakmul Biosphere Reserve.
laws.penalty: Environmental damage: fines up to 50,000 days minimum wage. Criminal prosecution: 1-9 years. Activity suspension in protected areas.
exceptions: Indigenous communities with traditional land rights may continue subsistence activities in some protected areas
Existing lawful activities may be grandfathered with restoration requirements
Research with SEMARNAT permits allowed

quiz.q: What percentage of all Earth's species can be found in Mexico, making it a megadiverse country?
quiz.explanation: Mexico is one of 17 'megadiverse' countries in the world, harboring approximately 10% of all species on Earth. Mexico has extraordinary biodiversity due to its range of ecosystems from deserts to cloud forests to coral reefs, as well as high levels of endemic species found nowhere else.

laws.title: UNAM Autonomy — National University
laws.subtitle: UNAM — constitutionally autonomous, tuition-free
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's National Autonomous University (UNAM) is the largest university in Latin America, with over 340,000 students. Its autonomy was established by law in 1929 after student strikes, and constitutionally recognized in 1980. UNAM has the right to self-governance, create its own legislation, and police cannot enter without rector's permission. Annual tuition is nominally 2 centavos per year — effectively free. UNAM provides free education to over 100,000 undergraduate students annually. It has produced 7 of Mexico's 13 Nobel laureates.
laws.penalty: Violations of UNAM's autonomy by government authorities: constitutional challenge. Campus crimes handled by internal security and judicial coordination.
exceptions: Private universities operate under separate regulatory framework
Students must pass UNAM entrance exam (very competitive)
Professional schools (law, medicine) have separate licensing requirements

quiz.q: What is the annual tuition at Mexico's UNAM, the largest university in Latin America?
quiz.explanation: UNAM's annual tuition is nominally 2 centavos — the symbolic minimum established by law. This effectively makes it free for students, though they pay modest fees for specific services. UNAM's autonomy and free tuition make it one of the most accessible major research universities in the world.

laws.title: INE — Electoral Institute Reforms
laws.subtitle: Instituto Nacional Electoral — independent electoral authority
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's INE (Instituto Nacional Electoral), formerly IFE, is an autonomous body that organizes federal elections. Created after decades of PRI electoral fraud, INE has been central to Mexico's democratic transition. The 2023 'Plan B' electoral reform by President AMLO attempted to reduce INE's powers and budget, but was struck down by the Supreme Court. A 2023 constitutional reform partially modified INE's structure. INE oversees voter registration, political financing, campaign regulations, and election day organization.
laws.penalty: Electoral law violations: administrative fines, candidate disqualification. Electoral fraud: criminal prosecution (7-14 years for officials).
exceptions: Internal party elections regulated by parties themselves with INE oversight
Local elections increasingly administered by INE under federal standards
Indigenous customary law (usos y costumbres) elections in Oaxaca have modified procedures

quiz.q: What was the predecessor institution to Mexico's INE?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's INE (Instituto Nacional Electoral) was previously called the IFE (Instituto Federal Electoral). Created in 1990 as an independent electoral authority after decades of PRI-controlled elections, it was renamed and restructured as INE in 2014 to take over administration of both federal and many state elections.

laws.title: Ley Federal de Armas de Fuego — Strict Gun Law
laws.subtitle: LFAFCE — only 1 legal gun store in Mexico (SEDENA)
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Ley Federal de Armas de Fuego y Explosivos restricts civilian firearms severely. There is only ONE legal gun store in all of Mexico — operated by SEDENA (army) in Mexico City. Civilians may possess limited calibers (.380 ACP and below, no .38 Special, no 9mm for civilians) at home only. Carry permits require extraordinary justification. Despite these restrictions, Mexico has extremely high firearm violence — over 30,000 murders annually — because illegal US-sourced weapons flood the country. Mexico sued US gun manufacturers in US federal court.
laws.penalty: Illegal firearm possession: 3-10 years. Carrying without permit: 3-8 years. Trafficking: 15-30 years.
exceptions: Hunters and sport shooters may possess certain calibers with permits
Security guards with licensed companies may carry
Military and police exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Ley Federal de Armas de Fuego y Explosivos

quiz.q: How many legal civilian gun stores exist in all of Mexico?
quiz.explanation: Mexico has exactly ONE legal civilian gun store — operated by SEDENA (the Mexican army) inside a military base in Mexico City. Despite these extremely strict laws, Mexico has very high gun violence because illegal firearms — primarily smuggled from the United States — are widely available to criminal organizations.

laws.title: Seguro Popular → IMSS-Bienestar
laws.subtitle: Healthcare for informal workers — universal access goal
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Seguro Popular (2004-2019) provided health insurance to workers not covered by IMSS (social security for formal workers). President AMLO replaced it with IMSS-Bienestar in 2020, aiming for universal free healthcare. The transition was chaotic — medicine shortages worsened and the new system struggled with infrastructure. Mexico's healthcare has a three-tier structure: IMSS (formal workers), ISSSTE (government workers), and IMSS-Bienestar (informal/uninsured). Approximately 40% of Mexico's workforce is informal.
laws.penalty: No penalties for patients. Healthcare fraud by providers: criminal prosecution, exclusion from public health systems.
exceptions: IMSS mandatory for formal employees (employer pays 70%, worker 25%, government 5%)
Private healthcare widely used by those who can afford it
International health emergencies may trigger additional coverage

quiz.q: What percentage of Mexico's workforce is estimated to be informal (without IMSS coverage)?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 40% of Mexico's workforce is informal — working without formal employment contracts and therefore without IMSS coverage. This large informal sector was the target of Seguro Popular (2004-2019), which AMLO replaced with IMSS-Bienestar in an attempt to provide universal healthcare coverage.

laws.title: Ejido System — Communal Land Tenure
laws.subtitle: Ejido lands: communal post-revolution agrarian reform
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's ejido system, created by the 1917 Constitution and implemented through agrarian reform (1934-1940), redistributed land from haciendas to rural communities. Ejidos are communal land holdings that can be used but originally could not be sold. The 1992 reform (Article 27 amendment) allowed ejidatarios to convert ejido land to private title. This enabled the expansion of maquiladoras and urban development on ejido land. Ejido land still covers about half of Mexico's rural territory. Land certification is managed by RAN (National Agrarian Registry).
laws.penalty: Irregular use of ejido land: ejido assembly proceedings. Fraudulent conversion: civil and criminal liability. Invasion of ejido land: criminal trespass.
exceptions: Ejidatarios may rent their parcels to third parties
Ejido common lands used for collective activities under assembly rules
PROCEDE program formalized individual ejido parcels

quiz.q: What did Mexico's 1992 reform to Article 27 allow ejidatarios to do for the first time?
options: Convert ejido land to private title (enable sale)
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 1992 reform to Article 27 of the Constitution allowed ejidatarios to convert their communal ejido land parcels to private title, enabling legal sale of previously inalienable land. This was a major shift from post-revolutionary land reform principles and opened ejido land to commercial development.

laws.title: SAT — Tax Authority & RFC Registration
laws.subtitle: Servicio de Administración Tributaria — mandatory registration
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's SAT (Servicio de Administración Tributaria) is the tax authority. All individuals earning income and all businesses must register and obtain an RFC (Registro Federal de Contribuyentes) tax ID. Mexico has a CFDI (digital tax invoice) system where all commercial transactions above certain thresholds require electronic invoicing. Tax evasion is widespread — Mexico's tax collection as % of GDP is among Latin America's lowest. Recent reforms expanded VAT to digital services (Netflix, Uber etc.) and required platforms to withhold taxes for gig workers.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: 3-9 years imprisonment. Late filing: surcharges 1.47%/month. Serious fraud: 9 years+.
exceptions: Small informal businesses below threshold have simplified RIF regime
Agricultural cooperatives have reduced tax rates
Export companies may recover input VAT

quiz.q: What does Mexico's RFC stand for in the context of tax registration?
quiz.explanation: RFC stands for Registro Federal de Contribuyentes — the federal taxpayer registration number required by Mexico's SAT. All individuals with income and all businesses must register with SAT to obtain an RFC. It functions as Mexico's tax identification number for all fiscal transactions.

laws.title: Sistema Acusatorio — Oral Criminal Trials
laws.subtitle: 2008 constitutional reform — adversarial criminal justice
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 2008 constitutional reform replaced the inquisitorial written criminal process with an oral adversarial system, fully implemented nationwide by 2016. The new system features: oral public trials, adversarial evidence presentation, presumption of innocence explicitly guaranteed, alternative dispute resolution, and restorative justice mechanisms. Pre-trial detention criteria were tightened. The reform also created the NSJP (New Criminal Justice System) and SETEC to train judges and lawyers. Despite the reform, trial delays and impunity remain major challenges.
laws.penalty: Violations of due process rights: evidence exclusion, case dismissal. Wrongful pre-trial detention: compensation.
exceptions: Organized crime cases handled under separate provisions with extended pre-trial detention
State courts implemented reform on different timelines
Some procedural elements differ between federal and state courts

quiz.q: By what year did Mexico's oral adversarial criminal justice system need to be fully implemented nationwide?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2008 constitutional reform mandated nationwide implementation of the oral adversarial criminal justice system by 2016. The reform replaced the centuries-old inquisitorial written process, introducing oral public trials, presumption of innocence protections, and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.

laws.title: Denominaciones de Origen — Tequila and Cultural Products
laws.subtitle: DO protections for tequila, mezcal, Oaxacan products
laws.fullDescription: Mexico has 16 Denominations of Origin (DOs) protecting products tied to specific regions: tequila (Jalisco region), mezcal, charanda, Oaxacan textiles, Olinalá lacquerware, and others. The Consejo Regulador del Tequila (CRT) certifies all tequila production — only agave spirits from designated Jalisco regions may be called tequila. Mexico actively defends these DOs internationally through WTO and bilateral agreements. The 2016 Mezcal Standard expanded mezcal's protected designation.
laws.penalty: Using protected DO names without authorization: civil fines, criminal prosecution for fraud, product seizure.
exceptions: Products labeled 'agave spirit' or 'Mexican spirit' (not DO name) may be sold
Artisanal producers have modified DO requirements in some categories
Grandfathered products from before DO establishment have transition periods
laws.sourceLabel: Instituto Mexicano de la Propiedad Industrial

quiz.q: Which Mexican agency certifies that tequila meets the Denomination of Origin standard?
quiz.explanation: The Consejo Regulador del Tequila (CRT) certifies all tequila production, ensuring compliance with Mexico's Denomination of Origin rules. Only blue agave spirits produced in the designated regions (mainly Jalisco) may legally be called tequila.

laws.title: Fiscalía General — Independent Prosecutor
laws.subtitle: FGR — constitutional autonomy from executive branch
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 2018 constitutional reform made the Attorney General's Office (FGR — Fiscalía General de la República) constitutionally autonomous, ending direct presidential control. The first autonomous Fiscal General serves a 9-year non-renewable term. This reform was intended to end the abuse of criminal prosecution as a political tool. The FGR handles federal crimes including organized crime, corruption, and human rights violations. The 2014 disappearance of 43 students from Ayotzinapa is among the FGR's highest-profile cases.
laws.penalty: FGR prosecutors who abuse prosecutorial powers face internal discipline and criminal prosecution.
exceptions: State-level crimes handled by state prosecutors (Fiscalías Estatales)
Military crimes handled by military justice system
Specialized anti-organized crime unit (SEIDO) has enhanced investigative powers

quiz.q: How long is the term of Mexico's Fiscal General (Attorney General) under the 2018 autonomy reform?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 2018 constitutional reform established a 9-year non-renewable term for the Fiscal General. The long non-renewable term is designed to insulate the office from political pressure — unlike the old Attorney General who served at presidential will and was replaced with each new administration.

laws.title: Vaquita Marina — Critically Endangered Protection
laws.subtitle: World's most endangered marine mammal — Gulf of California
laws.fullDescription: The vaquita marina (Phocoena sinus) is the world's most critically endangered marine mammal, endemic to Mexico's Upper Gulf of California. Fewer than 10 remain (2024). Vaquitas drown as bycatch in gillnets used for totoaba fish, whose swim bladder is illegally trafficked to China. Mexico has banned gillnet fishing in the vaquita's habitat, created a Zero Tolerance Area, and worked with international conservation groups. Cartels control totoaba trafficking. SEMARNAT leads recovery efforts.
laws.penalty: Illegal fishing in Zero Tolerance Area: heavy fines, vessel confiscation, criminal prosecution. Totoaba trafficking: organized crime penalties.
exceptions: Traditional artisanal fishing outside the Zero Tolerance Area with vaquita-safe gear
Scientific research permits for approved conservation programs
Indigenous fishing communities have some provisions for traditional practices

quiz.q: Why are vaquita marina porpoises critically endangered?
options: Drowning as bycatch in gillnets targeting totoaba fish
Climate change warming the Gulf of California
quiz.explanation: Vaquitas drown as bycatch (accidental catch) in gillnets set by illegal fishermen targeting the totoaba, whose swim bladder sells for up to $100,000 in Chinese black markets. Despite gillnet bans and enforcement, criminal cartels control totoaba trafficking, making vaquita conservation extremely difficult.

laws.title: IMSS — Social Security Mandatory Enrollment
laws.subtitle: IMSS covers formal workers: healthcare, pension, disability
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's IMSS (Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social), created in 1943, provides social security to formal sector workers including healthcare, disability insurance, maternity leave, daycare, and a pension (AFORE retirement accounts). Employer enrollment is mandatory for all formal workers. IMSS contributions are tripartite: employer (70%), worker (25%), government (5%). IMSS is among Mexico's largest employers with its own hospital network. The 1997 pension reform created individual AFORE accounts replacing the pay-as-you-go system.
laws.penalty: Employer failure to enroll workers: back contributions, fines, interest. IMSS fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Self-employed may voluntarily enroll in IMSS
Agricultural day laborers have modified enrollment options
Federal government workers covered by ISSSTE, not IMSS

quiz.q: When was Mexico's IMSS (social security institute) created?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's IMSS was created in 1943 under President Manuel Ávila Camacho, providing social security to formal sector workers. It covers healthcare, disability, maternity benefits, and pensions. IMSS is one of Latin America's largest social security institutions.

laws.title: Alcoholímetro — DUI Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Mexico City's zero-tolerance drunk driving checkpoints
laws.fullDescription: Mexico City (and many states) operate Alcoholímetro checkpoints — mobile breathalyzer enforcement units — particularly on weekend nights. Blood alcohol limit is 0.4g/L in Mexico City (lower in some states). Drivers who fail the breathalyzer are detained overnight (arraigo) without criminal charge under an administrative arrest. Refusing the test results in automatic detention. Mexico City's Alcoholímetro began in 2003 and reduced alcohol-related traffic deaths by over 60%.
laws.penalty: BAC above limit (0.4g/L): vehicle impoundment, overnight administrative detention, license suspension, fine.
exceptions: Drivers transporting medical patients to hospital may have expedited review
Designated driver programs recognized in some municipalities
Some states have higher BAC limits (0.8g/L)

quiz.q: What is Mexico City's blood alcohol limit for driving?
quiz.explanation: Mexico City's blood alcohol limit for driving is 0.4g/L. Drivers who fail the Alcoholímetro breathalyzer test face overnight administrative detention, vehicle impoundment, and license suspension. The program, started in 2003, has significantly reduced alcohol-related traffic deaths.

laws.title: Maquiladoras — Export Manufacturing
laws.subtitle: IMMEX program — duty-free assembly for export
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's maquiladora industry (IMMEX program) allows foreign companies to import materials duty-free, assemble goods in Mexico, and export the finished products — with Mexican labor and no duties on imported inputs. Maquiladoras operate primarily along the US-Mexico border (Tijuana, Juárez, Matamoros). USMCA updated maquiladora rules of origin. The sector employs over 2 million Mexicans, primarily in electronics, automotive parts, and textiles. Maquiladoras account for about 50% of Mexico's exports.
laws.penalty: IMMEX violations (selling duty-exempt goods domestically): full duties owed, fines, program cancellation.
exceptions: Goods may be sold in Mexico if full customs duties paid
Shelter companies allow small foreign firms to use maquiladora benefits without Mexican incorporation
USMCA rules of origin require significant content from North America

quiz.q: Approximately how many Mexicans does the maquiladora/IMMEX sector employ?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's maquiladora sector (IMMEX program) employs over 2 million workers, primarily along the US-Mexico border in cities like Tijuana, Ciudad Juárez, and Matamoros. The sector accounts for roughly 50% of Mexico's exports, focused on electronics, automotive parts, and medical devices.

laws.title: Ley de Aguas Nacionales — Water Rights
laws.subtitle: LAN — federal control over national water resources
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's Ley de Aguas Nacionales (LAN) establishes that water is national property managed by CONAGUA (National Water Commission). Water concessions are required for any use above domestic thresholds. Mexico faces severe water scarcity — 50 million lack adequate water access. A 2022 Supreme Court ruling recognized access to water as a fundamental right. Water overallocation in agricultural regions has depleted aquifers. Industrial water concessions to beverage companies (Coca-Cola, beer) have been controversial in drought-prone states.
laws.penalty: Water extraction without concession: fines, operations suspension, criminal prosecution. Contamination of national waters: 1-9 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Domestic use (small quantities for household) does not require concession
Indigenous communities have rights to water in traditional territories
Emergency water access cannot be denied by CONAGUA

quiz.q: Who owns water resources under Mexico's Ley de Aguas Nacionales?
options: The municipality where water is located
quiz.explanation: Mexico's Ley de Aguas Nacionales establishes that all water is national property — owned by the federal nation and managed by CONAGUA. Any use above domestic consumption thresholds requires a formal water concession from CONAGUA, regardless of whether the water is surface or groundwater.

laws.title: AFORE — Individual Retirement Accounts
laws.subtitle: 1997 pension reform — privatized defined contribution system
laws.fullDescription: Mexico's 1997 pension reform replaced the pay-as-you-go IMSS pension with individual AFORE (Administradoras de Fondos para el Retiro) accounts — defined contribution retirement savings managed by regulated private fund managers. Workers and employers contribute to individual accounts. A 2021 reform increased employer contributions from 5.15% to 13.875% of salary phased in through 2030 and eliminated the minimum pension guarantee limit. Workers may choose their AFORE from among 10+ licensed operators. AFORE assets exceed 5 trillion pesos (~$300 billion).
laws.penalty: AFORE fraud: criminal prosecution, fund manager license revocation. Failure to make mandatory contributions: IMSS enforcement.
exceptions: Workers hired before 1997 may choose between old and new pension calculation methods
ISSSTE (government worker) pension reform was separate (2007)
Voluntary savings contributions have tax advantages
laws.sourceLabel: CONSAR — Comisión Nacional del Sistema de Ahorro para el Retiro

quiz.q: In what year did Mexico shift from a pay-as-you-go pension to individual AFORE accounts?
quiz.explanation: Mexico's 1997 pension reform replaced the IMSS pay-as-you-go system with individual AFORE accounts — defined contribution retirement savings managed by regulated private fund managers. Workers hired before 1997 can choose between the old and new systems when they retire.
